entry.title: The New Kid on the Block in SAP's Integration Portfolio: SAP Managed File Transfer by Redwood
entry.content:
TechEd is now over – and I am quite happy that we got to experience so many different announcements, sessions and demo exercises related to SAP Integration Suite. If you missed any of it, my colleague Claire has pulled everything together on-demand in this blog post.

But one of the greatest things released in recent weeks, which deserves it’s own spotlight is the announcement that SAP Managed File Transfer by Redwood is an SAP Solution Extension. To make sure this news doesn't get lost in the jungle of post-TechEd content, we're hosting a dedicated Activation Webinar on it – and registration is already open here!

But just to set the stage: what is SAP Managed File Transfer, and why should you consider it?

File transfer - a stubborn gap in enterprise integration

Large files, strict audit requirements and external partners still make file transfer one of the most stubborn gaps in enterprise integration – and often the one that holds up an S/4HANA go-live.

Because APIs and events get most of the attention in integration conversations. Yet in almost every SAP landscape, a surprisingly large share of business-critical data still moves as files: such as payment and bank statement files, EDI documents with suppliers and customers, payroll exports, product and pricing catalogs, regulatory submissions and batch extracts for analytics.

And these requirements are hard to manage properly:

  • Size and volume. Multi-gigabyte files and high-volume batch runs push message-based integration platforms beyond what they're designed for.
  • Compliance. Regulations such as SOX, HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS require encryption, complete audit trails and defined retention – evidence that ad-hoc FTP servers and scripts rarely provide.
  • External partners. Banks, suppliers, logistics providers and authorities each bring their own protocols, keys and schedules. Onboarding every new partner often means another IT ticket, another script and another server nobody wants to own.

In many companies, the result is a patchwork of legacy SFTP servers, scheduled jobs and custom code, with little visibility into what was sent, when and to whom. And this patchwork tends to surface at the worst possible moment: during an S/4HANA transformation. When teams inventory their interfaces, file-based flows often turn out to be the largest and least-documented group – and with SAP Process Orchestration approaching the end of mainstream maintenance, they need a future-proof home.

SAP Managed File Transfer by Redwood closes that gap

As an SAP Solution Extension – co-sold, co-developed and co-supported by SAP – SAP Managed File Transfer (MFT) by Redwood handles what general-purpose integration platforms aren't built for: multi-gigabyte files, audit retention for SOX, HIPAA, GDPR and PCI-DSS, and partner self-service exchanges that don't need IT for every transfer.

Combined with SAP Integration Suite, it covers your full integration architecture under a single SAP relationship.

What you are going to learn in this upcoming webinar

  • What SAP MFT is and why it completes SAP's integration architecture
  • Where it matters – the use cases across Manufacturing, Retail, Banking, Life Sciences and the Public Sector where it makes the difference
  • How to move forward with SAP and partners

I hope these couple of statements are enough to get you excited – at least I am already convinced 🙂 So make sure that you register for our upcoming session to learn more and get in touch with our experts:

Register for the SAP Managed File Transfer Activation Webinar

See you there! And if you already want to learn more about this Solution Extension before the webinar, I can recommend following ressources:

 

  • Website on SAP Managed File Transfer by Redwood
  • A brief solution demo on this new capability 
  • Whitepaper:  File transfer operations for your cloud transformation

 

Stay tuned!

entry.title: Re: Collective run VL10A does not work properly for item...
entry.content:
Based on the symptoms, the issue is likely not the batch determination strategy itself, but the availability of stock, batch split execution, or delivery creation logic in VL10A.

A concise expert response would be:

For material 3105001000 (Hipmap), if batch determination is active and deliveries are created through VL10A, then each delivery should receive batch assignments according to the configured batch search strategy and available stock.

Since you observe:

  • One delivery with no batch assignment
  • One delivery with fewer batches than expected

I would recommend checking the following points:

 Batch Determination Log

For the affected delivery, go to:

VL03N

→ Item

→ Environment

→ Batch Determination Analysis

Check whether:

  • No batches were found.
  • Batches were excluded by selection criteria.
  • Required quantity could not be covered.

 

  1. Available Batch Stock

Review stock at batch level:

MMBE

Verify:

  • Unrestricted stock exists for all expected batches.
  • Stock is available in the same plant/storage location used by the delivery.
  • No stock is already reserved by other sales orders or deliveries.

 

  1. Batch Split Configuration

Check whether:

SPRO

→ Logistics Execution

→ Shipping

→ Deliveries

→ Batch Split

allows automatic batch splitting during delivery creation.

If batch split is not permitted, the system may assign only one batch or leave part of the quantity unassigned.

 

  1. Delivery Creation in VL10A

VL10A processes multiple orders sequentially. If stock is limited:

  • Earlier deliveries may consume preferred batches.
  • Later deliveries may receive reduced quantities.
  • Some deliveries may not receive any batch assignment.

Therefore, the sequence of delivery creation should be reviewed.

 

  1. Check Incompletion and Delivery Log

VL03N

→ Environment

→ Log

Look for messages such as:

  • No batch found
  • Required quantity not available
  • Batch split not possible
  • Availability check restrictions

 

  1. Verify Search Strategy

Check the batch search procedure:

VCH1 / COB1

and confirm:

  • Correct search procedure is assigned.
  • Sort rule is working as intended (e.g., FIFO, FEFO).
  • Selection class characteristics do not exclude valid batches.

 Most commonly, this behavior occurs because available batch stock is consumed by earlier deliveries during VL10A processing, leaving insufficient stock for subsequent deliveries, or because automatic batch split is not able to cover the requested quantity. The batch determination analysis log for the affected delivery item will usually reveal the exact reason.

entry.title: Re: In the SAP Cloud Data Migration Cockpit (DMC) downloa...
entry.content:
Hi, 

Thanks for your query.

The value ETE;80;0;C;80;0 in Row 6 of the DMC template uses the following structure:
- ETE indicates a text field.
- 80 is the field length on the source side — the maximum number of characters allowed in the template for that field.
- 0 represents the number of decimal places.
- C is the data type (Char).

The second instance of 80;0 can be disregarded.

Best regards,
Peter

entry.title: Re: Context issues when opening EPM workbooks with "Refresh on Opening" from a BPF.
entry.content:
First, open the Registry Editor with administrative privileges. Navigate to the following paths and ensure their LoadBehavior value is set to 3
1. HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\Excel\Addins\SapExcelAddIn
2. HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\Excel\Addins\FPMXLClient.Connect

Then navigate to the following paths and ensure their SapCreateKey is set to 3
1.HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\SAP.AO.Xl.Launch
2.HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\SAP.AO.Xl.Launch\shell\Open\command

Once these values are updated, open Microsoft Excel. You should now see the EPM and Data Manager tabs activated in the ribbon, as well as a new "Analysis" option under the File menu.
After this templates must open in the same excel session(I faced the same issues with some installations and had to change registry values in order to fix Analysis load behavior). If the above doesn't work you could also check this parameter "/app XLS /UseRunningProcess" that sets Analysis Add-In to start using a Microsoft Excel process that is already running.

You can find the instructions here: https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_BUSINESSOBJECTS_ANALYSIS_OFFICE/df90d3701aba42b9a4351caa387bd672/f26e754f6c9b1014bf2c9a7eb0e91070.html?locale=en-US&q=Userunningprocess

entry.title: My First SAP RAP Application – Part 3: Building a Student Management App Using Unmanaged RAP
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community! 👋

Welcome to Part 3 of my SAP RAP learning journey!

In my previous blog posts, I shared my experience building a Student Management Application using the SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP).

In Part 1, I created my first Student Management Application using Managed RAP, starting from the database table and CDS View Entities and ending with a SAP Fiori Elements application.

Part 1: https://community.sap.com/t5/abap-blog-posts/my-first-sap-rap-application-building-a-student-management-app-using/ba-p/14506725

In Part 2, I enhanced the application with Selection Fields, Validations, Determinations, Custom Actions, and Draft Handling.

Part 2: https://community.sap.com/t5/abap-blog-posts/my-first-sap-rap-application-part-2-advanced-rap-features-with-managed-rap/ba-p/14507282My First SAP RAP Application – Part 2: Advanced RAP Features with Managed RAP

After practicing these features, I wanted to understand something more deeply:

What happens when the RAP framework does not automatically implement Create, Update, and Delete operations?

That question encouraged me to start learning Unmanaged RAP.

In this blog, I will share how I rebuilt the same Student Management scenario using an Unmanaged Business Object, focusing on the CRUD implementation, transactional buffer, and save sequence.

1. Managed vs. Unmanaged RAP

Before starting the development, let's understand the main difference between the two implementation types.

Managed RAP

In Managed RAP, the framework provides the standard transactional implementation.

For example, when we define:

create;
update;
delete;

the framework can automatically manage the standard CRUD operations and persistence.

The developer mainly focuses on the business-specific logic.

Unmanaged RAP

In Unmanaged RAP, the developer implements the required transactional operations in the Behavior Pool.

This includes:

  • Create

  • Update

  • Delete

  • Read

  • Transactional Buffer Handling

  • Save Sequence

  • Locking and Authorization

Unmanaged RAP is particularly useful when we want to integrate existing business logic, such as APIs or function modules, into a RAP Business Object.

For learning purposes, I decided to implement a simple custom Student Management scenario.

Quick Comparison

Feature Managed RAP Unmanaged RAP

CRUD implementationHandled by the frameworkImplemented by the developer
Transactional BufferFramework-managedDeveloper-managed
PersistenceStandard framework implementationCustom save implementation
Number generationCan use managed numberingCan be implemented manually
Fiori ElementsSupportedSupported

2. Development Environment

For this project, I am using:

  • SAP S/4HANA 2023 FPS01 — On-Premise

  • ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse

  • ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model

  • Unmanaged Business Object

  • SAP Fiori Elements

To keep my original Managed RAP application unchanged, I created a separate set of development objects.

Development Objects

Object Name

Database TableZUM_STD_TABLE
Interface CDS ViewZ_I_UM_STD
Projection CDS ViewZ_C_UM_STD
Base Behavior DefinitionZ_I_UM_STD
Behavior PoolZBP_I_UM_STD
Projection Behavior DefinitionZ_C_UM_STD
Metadata ExtensionZ_M_UM_STD
Service DefinitionZ_SD_UM_STD
OData V4 UI BindingZ_UI_UM_STD_O4

Let's start!

3. Creating the Database Table

The first step was creating the database table to store student information.

I created a table named ZUM_STD_TABLE.

@EndUserText.label : 'Unmanaged Student Table'
@AbapCatalog.enhancement.category : #NOT_EXTENSIBLE
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #A
@AbapCatalog.dataMaintenance : #ALLOWED

define table zum_std_table {

  key client       : abap.clnt not null;
  key rollno       : sysuuid_x16 not null;

  studentname      : abap.char(100);
  studentclass     : abap.char(2);
  studentage       : abap.numc(3);
  schoolname       : abap.char(150);

}

The table contains the same main business fields as my first Managed RAP application.

rollno is the technical key, stored as a UUID.

The most important difference will appear later: in this Unmanaged implementation, I generate the UUID in my own Create logic.

Figure 1: Database table created for the Unmanaged Student Management Application.

4. Creating the Interface CDS View

Next, I created the root Interface CDS View Entity Z_I_UM_STD.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Unmanaged Student Interface'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true

define root view entity Z_I_UM_STD
  as select from zum_std_table
{
  key rollno       as Rollno,
      studentname  as Studentname,
      studentclass as Studentclass,
      studentage   as Studentage,
      schoolname   as Schoolname
}

Explanation

  • define root view entity identifies the root entity of our Business Object.

  • ZUM_STD_TABLE is the underlying database table.

  • The fields are exposed using meaningful CDS element names.

At this stage, the implementation looks almost identical to Managed RAP.

The difference between Managed and Unmanaged is not in the CDS View itself, but in how the Business Object behavior is implemented.

Figure 2: Root Interface CDS View Entity for the Student Business Object.

5. Creating the Projection CDS View

After creating the Interface CDS View, I created the Projection CDS View Z_C_UM_STD.

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Unmanaged Student Projection'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
@Metadata.allowExtensions: true

define root view entity Z_C_UM_STD
  as projection on Z_I_UM_STD
{
  key Rollno,
      Studentname,
      Studentclass,
      Studentage,
      Schoolname
}

The Projection CDS View determines which fields are exposed to the service consumer.

Later, we will use a Metadata Extension to control how these fields appear in SAP Fiori Elements.

Figure 3: Projection CDS View exposing the Student Business Object.

6. Creating the Unmanaged Base Behavior Definition

This is where the real difference begins.

In my previous Managed RAP project, I used:

managed implementation in class zbp_i_std unique;

This time, I used an Unmanaged implementation.

unmanaged implementation in class zbp_i_um_std unique;
strict ( 2 );

define behavior for Z_I_UM_STD alias Student
  lock master
  authorization master ( instance )
{
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  field ( readonly ) Rollno;
}

Explanation

unmanaged implementation

Indicates that the application developer is responsible for implementing the required transactional behavior.

create; update; delete;

Defines the operations supported by the Business Object.

lock master

Declares that the Business Object requires a locking implementation.

authorization master ( instance )

Declares instance-level authorization handling.

field ( readonly ) Rollno

Prevents the consumer from directly entering or modifying the UUID.

Unlike the Managed scenario, I did not define a persistent table for automatic framework persistence. Instead, I implemented database persistence in the saver class.

Figure 4: Unmanaged Behavior Definition with CRUD operations.

7. Generating the Behavior Pool

Next, I generated the Behavior Implementation in Eclipse ADT.

Behavior Pool:

ZBP_I_UM_STD

Eclipse generated a local handler class with methods similar to the following:

CLASS lhc_Student DEFINITION
  INHERITING FROM cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  PRIVATE SECTION.

    METHODS get_instance_authorizations
      FOR INSTANCE AUTHORIZATION
      IMPORTING keys
      REQUEST requested_authorizations
      FOR Student
      RESULT result.

    METHODS create FOR MODIFY
      IMPORTING entities FOR CREATE Student.

    METHODS update FOR MODIFY
      IMPORTING entities FOR UPDATE Student.

    METHODS delete FOR MODIFY
      IMPORTING keys FOR DELETE Student.

    METHODS read FOR READ
      IMPORTING keys FOR READ Student
      RESULT result.

    METHODS lock FOR LOCK
      IMPORTING keys FOR LOCK Student.

ENDCLASS.

I also received a local saver class containing methods such as:

  • FINALIZE

  • CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE

  • SAVE

  • CLEANUP

  • CLEANUP_FINALIZE

These methods represent different parts of the Unmanaged RAP transactional lifecycle.

Handler vs. Saver

The Handler Class processes requests during the interaction phase.

The Saver Class is responsible for the save sequence, including persisting buffered changes.

This separation was one of the most interesting concepts I learned in Unmanaged RAP.

Figure 5: Local Behavior Handler and Saver classes generated by Eclipse.

8. Creating a Transactional Buffer

Before implementing the CRUD methods, I needed somewhere to store changes temporarily.

In Managed RAP, the framework maintains the transactional buffer.

In Unmanaged RAP, the application implementation needs to maintain the relevant transactional state.

For my learning example, I created a simple local buffer class:

CLASS lcl_buffer DEFINITION FINAL.
  PUBLIC SECTION.

    CLASS-DATA gt_create TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zum_std_table
                         WITH EMPTY KEY.

    CLASS-DATA gt_update TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zum_std_table
                         WITH EMPTY KEY.

    CLASS-DATA gt_delete TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF sysuuid_x16
                         WITH EMPTY KEY.

ENDCLASS.

CLASS lcl_buffer IMPLEMENTATION.
ENDCLASS.

Understanding the Buffer

Internal Table Purpose

gt_createStores newly created students
gt_updateStores modified student data
gt_deleteStores student keys marked for deletion

For example, when a Create request arrives, the student data is first stored in gt_create.

It is not immediately inserted into the database.

The database operation takes place later during the save sequence.

Transactional Flow

Create / Update / Delete Request

↓

Behavior Handler

↓

Transactional Buffer

↓

Save Sequence

↓

Database Table

This simple buffer is intended for learning. A production implementation needs more complete handling of consistency, locks, errors, and transactional state.

Figure 6: A simple transactional buffer for Create, Update, and Delete operations.

9. Implementing the CREATE Method

Now we can start implementing the CRUD operations manually.

The first method is CREATE.

In this method, I generate the student's UUID, prepare the student record, store it in the buffer, and return the generated key to RAP.

METHOD create.

  LOOP AT entities INTO DATA(ls_entity).

    DATA lv_rollno TYPE sysuuid_x16.

    TRY.
        lv_rollno =
          cl_system_uuid=>create_uuid_x16_static( ).

      CATCH cx_uuid_error.

        APPEND VALUE #(
          %cid = ls_entity-%cid
        ) TO failed-Student.

        APPEND VALUE #(
          %cid = ls_entity-%cid
          %msg = new_message_with_text(
            severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
            text     = 'Failed to generate student UUID'
          )
        ) TO reported-Student.

        CONTINUE.

    ENDTRY.

    DATA(ls_student) = VALUE zum_std_table(
      rollno       = lv_rollno
      studentname  = ls_entity-Studentname
      studentclass = ls_entity-Studentclass
      studentage   = ls_entity-Studentage
      schoolname   = ls_entity-Schoolname
    ).

    APPEND ls_student TO lcl_buffer=>gt_create.

    APPEND VALUE #(
      %cid   = ls_entity-%cid
      Rollno = lv_rollno
    ) TO mapped-Student.

  ENDLOOP.

ENDMETHOD.

How Does It Work?

Step 1 — Receive Student Data

The entities parameter contains the instances requested for creation.

Step 2 — Generate UUID

I use:

cl_system_uuid=>create_uuid_x16_static( )

to generate the student key.

Step 3 — Store Data in the Buffer

APPEND ls_student TO lcl_buffer=>gt_create.

At this point, the record is not yet saved to the database.

Step 4 — Return the Generated Key

The mapped-Student response connects the request's %cid to the generated Rollno.

This helps the RAP framework identify the newly created instance.

Key Learning

In Managed RAP, I could use framework-managed numbering.

In this Unmanaged example, I implemented UUID generation myself.

10. Implementing the READ Method

The next method is READ.

A key point I learned is that reading data in a transactional scenario is not always the same as selecting records directly from the database.

For example, a student might have been created or updated during the current transaction without being saved yet.

Therefore, my READ implementation needs to consider the current transactional buffer.

The simplified lookup logic follows this order:

  1. Check whether the student is marked for deletion.

  2. Look for newly created data in gt_create.

  3. Look for modified data in gt_update.

  4. If the instance is not in the buffer, read it from the database.

  5. Return the current student data or report that it was not found.

A representative part of the implementation is:

IF line_exists(
  lcl_buffer=>gt_create[ rollno = ls_key-Rollno ]
).

  ls_student =
    lcl_buffer=>gt_create[ rollno = ls_key-Rollno ].

ELSEIF line_exists(
  lcl_buffer=>gt_update[ rollno = ls_key-Rollno ]
).

  ls_student =
    lcl_buffer=>gt_update[ rollno = ls_key-Rollno ].

ELSEIF line_exists(
  lt_db_students[ rollno = ls_key-Rollno ]
).

  ls_student =
    lt_db_students[ rollno = ls_key-Rollno ].

ENDIF.

The complete READ method also handles deleted or missing instances and fills the RAP result table.

Key Learning

The READ implementation must reflect the current transactional state.

Also, the query used to populate a Fiori List Report is not necessarily handled by this FOR READ method. The CDS-based query and transactional instance READ have different responsibilities.

11. Implementing the UPDATE Method

Next, I implemented the Update operation.

This method was interesting because RAP provides a special %control structure.

What Is %control?

Imagine a student has these values:

Field Current Value

StudentnameAhmed
StudentclassA1
Studentage20
SchoolnameAEA

Now the user changes only the age to 21.

We should update the age without unintentionally changing the other fields.

This is where %control becomes useful.

IF ls_entity-%control-Studentname =
   if_abap_behv=>mk-on.

  <ls_student>-studentname =
    ls_entity-Studentname.

ENDIF.

IF ls_entity-%control-Studentclass =
   if_abap_behv=>mk-on.

  <ls_student>-studentclass =
    ls_entity-Studentclass.

ENDIF.

IF ls_entity-%control-Studentage =
   if_abap_behv=>mk-on.

  <ls_student>-studentage =
    ls_entity-Studentage.

ENDIF.

IF ls_entity-%control-Schoolname =
   if_abap_behv=>mk-on.

  <ls_student>-schoolname =
    ls_entity-Schoolname.

ENDIF.

Before applying these changes, my method retrieves the current student state from the buffer or database.

After applying the requested field changes, the updated record remains in gt_update or, for a newly created instance, in gt_create.

Key Learning

%control identifies which fields are included in the modification request.

It helps implement partial updates correctly rather than blindly overwriting every field.

12. Implementing the DELETE Method

For Delete, I followed the same transactional principle.

Instead of immediately deleting the database record inside METHOD DELETE, I record the requested deletion in the buffer.

The method also handles different cases:

Case 1 — Newly Created Student

If the student is present only in gt_create, I remove it from that buffer because no database record exists yet.

Case 2 — Existing Student

If the student already exists, I store its UUID in gt_delete so it can be deleted during the save sequence.

Case 3 — Previously Updated Student

If the student has a pending update, I remove that update and keep the delete request as the final change.

For an existing student, the important buffering operation is:

DELETE lcl_buffer=>gt_update
  WHERE rollno = ls_key-Rollno.

APPEND ls_key-Rollno
  TO lcl_buffer=>gt_delete.

The complete method also verifies that the requested instance exists and returns a failure when necessary.

Key Learning

In Unmanaged RAP, the Delete method can prepare the deletion without immediately changing the database.

13. Implementing the SAVE Method

This was one of the most important parts of my Unmanaged RAP learning experience.

After implementing the interaction methods, I still needed to persist the buffered changes.

This happens in the Saver Class.

I implemented the SAVE method as follows:

METHOD save.

  " Save newly created students
  IF lcl_buffer=>gt_create IS NOT INITIAL.

    INSERT zum_std_table
      FROM TABLE @lcl_buffer=>gt_create.

  ENDIF.

  " Save updated students
  IF lcl_buffer=>gt_update IS NOT INITIAL.

    UPDATE zum_std_table
      FROM TABLE @lcl_buffer=>gt_update.

  ENDIF.

  " Delete students
  LOOP AT lcl_buffer=>gt_delete
    INTO DATA(lv_rollno).

    DELETE FROM zum_std_table
      WHERE rollno = @lv_rollno.

  ENDLOOP.

ENDMETHOD.

How Does It Work?

The Saver processes the three buffer tables:

Buffer Database Operation

gt_createINSERT
gt_updateUPDATE
gt_deleteDELETE

Important Concept: Save Sequence

RAP separates the interaction phase from the save sequence.

The typical lifecycle includes:

Interaction Phase

Receive and process Create, Update, and Delete requests.

↓

FINALIZE

Perform final processing when required.

↓

CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE

Check whether the buffered changes can be saved consistently.

↓

SAVE

Persist the changes.

↓

CLEANUP

Clear temporary transaction data.

The CHECK_BEFORE_SAVE step is especially important because SAP RAP reaches the point-of-no-return after the relevant save checks succeed. A robust Unmanaged implementation must ensure persistence can complete successfully from that point onward.

My current Save implementation is a basic educational example. Before using it in production, the consistency checks and persistence error handling need to be strengthened.

Another important rule is that we should not execute COMMIT WORK directly inside the RAP Save method. Transaction completion is coordinated by the RAP transactional runtime.

14. Implementing CLEANUP

After the save sequence, we need to clear the transactional buffer.

I implemented the following method:

METHOD cleanup.

  CLEAR lcl_buffer=>gt_create.
  CLEAR lcl_buffer=>gt_update.
  CLEAR lcl_buffer=>gt_delete.

ENDMETHOD.

This prevents temporary data from a completed transaction from being reused by a later transaction in the same ABAP session.

Key Learning

Creating a buffer is only one part of unmanaged transaction handling.

We also need to manage its complete lifecycle, including cleanup.

15. Instance Authorization and Locking

In my Base Behavior Definition, I declared:

lock master
authorization master ( instance )

For the initial learning implementation, I added a simplified instance authorization method:

METHOD get_instance_authorizations.

  result = VALUE #(
    FOR key IN keys
    (
      %tky    = key-%tky
      %update = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
      %delete = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed
    )
  ).

ENDMETHOD.

This allows Update and Delete during development.

However, it is important to understand that this is not a real authorization check.

A production application must validate the user's actual permissions before allowing business operations.

What About Locking?

In Unmanaged RAP, a declared lock master requires a proper lock implementation.

For this learning stage, I focused first on understanding CRUD, buffering, and persistence. The locking implementation remains an item to complete before treating the application as fully functional.

An empty LOCK method does not provide concurrency protection.

16. Creating the Projection Behavior Definition

After implementing the Base Behavior, I created the Projection Behavior Definition for Z_C_UM_STD.

projection;
strict ( 2 );

define behavior for Z_C_UM_STD alias Student
{
  use create;
  use update;
  use delete;
}

The distinction is similar to Managed RAP:

  • The Base Behavior Definition declares the operations.

  • The Projection Behavior Definition exposes the selected operations to service consumers.

Notice that we use:

use create;
use update;
use delete;

rather than defining the operations again.

17. Creating the Metadata Extension

Next, I wanted to display the student fields in a SAP Fiori Elements List Report.

I created the Metadata Extension Z_M_UM_STD.

@Metadata.layer: #CORE
annotate entity Z_C_UM_STD with
{
  @UI.facet: [{
    id: 'StudentDetails',
    type: #IDENTIFICATION_REFERENCE,
    label: 'Student Details',
    position: 10
  }]

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 10, label: 'Roll Number' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 10, label: 'Roll Number' }]
  Rollno;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 20, label: 'Student Name' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 20, label: 'Student Name' }]
  @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }]
  Studentname;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 30, label: 'Student Class' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 30, label: 'Student Class' }]
  @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
  Studentclass;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 40, label: 'Student Age' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 40, label: 'Student Age' }]
  Studentage;

  @UI.lineItem: [{ position: 50, label: 'School Name' }]
  @UI.identification: [{ position: 50, label: 'School Name' }]

}

Explanation

@UI.lineItem

Defines columns in the Fiori List Report.

@UI.identification

Defines fields in the Object Page.

@UI.selectionField

Adds fields to the Filter Bar.

@UI.facet

Defines a section in the Object Page.

One thing I like about RAP is that the Fiori UI annotations work in a similar way for both Managed and Unmanaged implementations.

18. Creating the Service Definition

Next, I created a Service Definition named Z_SD_UM_STD.

@EndUserText.label: 'Unmanaged Student Service'

define service Z_SD_UM_STD {
  expose Z_C_UM_STD;
}

The Service Definition exposes the Projection CDS View to service consumers.

Just like in my previous Managed RAP application, I did not need to implement the OData protocol manually.

The service is exposed through the SAP RAP service infrastructure.

19. Creating the Service Binding and Opening Fiori

After activating the Service Definition, I created the following Service Binding:

Setting Value

Service BindingZ_UI_UM_STD_O4
Binding TypeOData V4 - UI
Service DefinitionZ_SD_UM_STD

I activated and published the service, then opened the Fiori Elements preview.

The List Report was generated successfully.

It displayed the expected columns:

  • Roll Number

  • Student Name

  • Student Class

  • Student Age

  • School Name

The filter fields for Student Name and Student Class also appeared.

Figure 17: Fiori Elements List Report generated from the Unmanaged RAP service.

An Issue I Encountered

Although the List Report opened, the Create button did not appear in the initial OData V4 UI preview.

This was an important reminder that activating the backend objects and opening the List Report does not automatically confirm that every transactional operation is available in the UI.

The application was built without Draft Handling, and I decided to explore an OData V2 UI binding for this non-draft scenario.

The Create, Update, and Delete operations still require end-to-end verification, including the remaining locking and save consistency requirements.

I prefer documenting this distinction rather than treating an opened Fiori screen as proof that the complete CRUD application has been tested successfully.

20. What I Learned from Unmanaged RAP

Working on this project helped me understand several concepts that were less visible when I first worked with Managed RAP.

1. CRUD Requires Explicit Implementation

In Managed RAP, I could define the standard operations and rely on the framework to implement them.

In Unmanaged RAP, I implemented the interaction methods myself.

2. The Transactional Buffer Is Important

A modification request does not necessarily mean an immediate database change.

The buffer maintains the current transactional state until the save sequence.

3. READ Must Consider Pending Changes

The current Business Object state may contain new, updated, or deleted instances that are not yet reflected in the database.

4. %control Helps with Partial Updates

It tells the implementation which fields were included in the modification request.

5. Handler and Saver Have Different Responsibilities

The Handler manages transactional interaction.

The Saver is responsible for save-sequence processing and persistence.

6. Unmanaged RAP Requires More Responsibility

Implementing CRUD is only the beginning.

Locking, authorization, consistency checks, error handling, and transactional cleanup are all important parts of a reliable Unmanaged Business Object.

21. Current Result and Next Steps

At this stage, I have created and activated the main development objects for the Unmanaged Student Management scenario.

I have also implemented the initial logic for:

  • CREATE

  • READ

  • UPDATE

  • DELETE

  • Transactional Buffer

  • SAVE

  • CLEANUP

  • Simplified Instance Authorization

The OData service has been published, and the Fiori Elements List Report has been displayed.

The remaining work includes completing the Lock implementation, strengthening save consistency checks, and verifying the full Create, Update, and Delete lifecycle through the UI.

This means the project is currently a hands-on Unmanaged RAP learning implementation, rather than a production-ready Business Object.

My Personal Experience

After completing my first Student Management Application using Managed RAP, I wanted to challenge myself by rebuilding the same application using Unmanaged RAP.

At first, I thought the difference would be mainly in the Behavior Definition. However, as I started implementing the application in Eclipse, I realized that Unmanaged RAP requires a deeper understanding of how transactional operations work.

One of the most interesting parts was implementing the CREATE method manually. Instead of relying on the framework to handle the operation, I had to generate the student UUID, prepare the record, store it in a transactional buffer, and return the generated key to RAP.

I also learned the importance of the %control structure while implementing UPDATE, because it allows us to modify only the fields included in the request.

Another valuable experience was working with the transactional buffer and the SAVE method. Understanding why changes are stored temporarily before being persisted helped me see what the Managed RAP framework normally handles behind the scenes.

Of course, I faced some challenges during development. For example, I encountered an error related to the GT_UPDATE buffer declaration, which I resolved by reviewing the buffer class and its definitions.

Later, when I published the OData V4 service and opened the application in SAP Fiori Elements, the List Report and filter fields appeared correctly, but the Create button was missing. This encouraged me to explore the differences between draft and non-draft applications and the available OData UI service bindings.

I am still working on completing the remaining implementation details and verifying the CRUD operations end-to-end.

Overall, this experience has helped me understand RAP beyond simply creating development objects. Writing the transactional logic myself gave me a much clearer picture of the responsibilities involved in Unmanaged RAP.

I believe that practicing both Managed and Unmanaged RAP is an important step toward becoming more confident in SAP RAP development.

AI disclosure: I used ChatGPT to help structure the article, improve the English writing, and understand technical concepts. The development and troubleshooting steps described here were performed hands-on in Eclipse and SAP Fiori Elements. Full end-to-end CRUD testing is still in progress.


Conclusion

Rebuilding my Student Management Application with Unmanaged RAP has helped me understand what happens behind the standard CRUD operations that Managed RAP normally handles for us.

The most valuable part of this experience was learning how the transactional buffer connects the Behavior Handler to the Saver Class.

I also learned that generating a Fiori Elements application is only one part of the overall implementation. Reliable transactional behavior requires correct backend handling throughout the complete lifecycle.

For me, this project is an important next step in understanding the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model.

I hope sharing this learning experience helps other beginners who are moving from Managed RAP to Unmanaged RAP.

Thank you for reading!

  2. SAP Help Portal — RAP Save Sequence Runtime

  3. Part 1 — Student Management Using Managed RAP

  4. Part 2 — Advanced RAP Features with Managed RAP

entry.title: Supplier invoice via BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CREATE1: keeping the payment terms key AND forcing the due
entry.content:
Lessons learned from building an inbound supplier-invoice API on SAP S/4HANA (on-premise / private cloud)

The business scenario

A procurement system outside SAP is where users capture supplier invoices. Each invoice is sent to S/4HANA as a JSON message and posted as a logistics invoice, exactly as if an AP clerk had entered it in MIRO:

External system ──JSON──▶ Inbound API (ABAP) ──▶ BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CREATE1 ──▶ RBKP/RSEG + FI document

Most of the message is what you would expect: purchase order and item, goods receipt reference, quantity, amount, tax lines. One requirement turned out to be harder than it looked.

The external system sends a concrete due date (dueDate).
SAP must still carry the payment terms key that comes from the purchase order (for example P001 – 7 days net).
The vendor line must fall due exactly on dueDate.

Example: document date 01.10., the PO payment terms are 7 days net, and dueDate = 26.10.
Expected result: payment terms key P001, baseline date 01.10., days 25, net due date 26.10.

In MIRO a user can do this by hand: enter the terms key, then overwrite the days on the Payment tab. Through the BAPI, it does not work out of the box.

Attempt 1: a 0-day terms key with baseline date = due date

The first version sent a 0-day terms key (P000) and set BLINE_DATE = dueDate. The net due date was correct, but the business rejected it. The invoice no longer carried the real terms key, and the baseline date no longer matched the document date.

Attempt 2: send the key and the days together

ls_header-pmnttrms   = 'P001'.            " key from PO
ls_header-bline_date = lv_document_date.  " baseline = document date
ls_header-dsct_days1 = lv_due - lv_doc.   " 25 days

Result:

M8 366  Terms of payment are incorrect. Either fill code or days/percentage.

What the standard code actually does

Reading the function group MRM_BAPI and the core function MRM_INVOICE_CREATE showed three separate gates. You have to get past all three.

# Where What it does

1LMRM_BAPIF0Q, header import checkPMNTTRMS or DSCT_DAYS1/2, NETTERMS, DSCT_PCT1/2, never both. Otherwise message M8 366.
2LMRM_BAPIF0C, mrm_invoice_create_callSets the local flag f_fix_payment_terms. If ZTERM is filled, the flag is cleared ("zterm will be dissolved").
3MRM_INVOICE_CHECKIf the flag is initial and ZTERM is filled, FI_TERMS_OF_PAYMENT_PROPOSE recalculates the days from T052 and your days are overwritten. Form MRM_RBKPV_CHECK also raises an error (message 607) if days are filled while the flag is initial.

So the BAPI interface itself allows "key only" or "days only". It has no parameter for "key plus fixed days".

The solution: two small implicit enhancements

The trick is to hand the BAPI only the days, then put the key back after gate 1, and tell gate 2 to keep the days.

Enhancement 1: after the header check, before posting

Enhancement point BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CREATE_02 in BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CREATE runs after RBKPV_FILL, while S_RBKPV can still be changed.

ENHANCEMENT 1.
  zcl_xx_iv_writer=>apply_zterm( CHANGING cs_rbkpv = s_rbkpv ).
ENDENHANCEMENT.
METHOD apply_zterm.
  IF gv_fix_terms = abap_true AND gv_zterm IS NOT INITIAL.
    cs_rbkpv-zterm = gv_zterm.          " put the key back
  ENDIF.
ENDMETHOD.

Enhancement 2: keep the days

Enhancement point MRM_INVOICE_CREATE_CALL_01 in LMRM_BAPIF0C sits just before the call to MRM_INVOICE_CREATE.

ENHANCEMENT 1.
  zcl_xx_iv_writer=>apply_fix_terms( CHANGING cv_fix = f_fix_payment_terms ).
ENDENHANCEMENT.
METHOD apply_fix_terms.
  IF gv_fix_terms = abap_true.
    cv_fix = abap_true.                 " do not re-propose days from T052
  ENDIF.
ENDMETHOD.

The calling code

" header: days only -> passes the M8 366 check
ls_header-bline_date = is_doc-header-bldat.
ls_header-dsct_days1 = is_doc-header-due_date - is_doc-header-bldat.

" remember the key for the enhancements
gv_zterm     = lv_zterm.                " sender > PO > vendor > nearest T052
gv_fix_terms = abap_true.
CLEAR ls_header-pmnttrms.

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_INCOMINGINVOICE_CREATE1' ...

CLEAR: gv_zterm, gv_fix_terms.          " MIRO and other callers never see the flag

Both enhancements are a single line that calls a static method in our own class. The logic can be tested and changed without touching the enhancement, and every other caller (MIRO, other interfaces, IDoc) sees empty buffers and behaves as standard.

Result

Field Value

Vendor line BSEG-ZTERMP001
ZFBDT (baseline)01.10.
ZBD1T (days)25
BSEG-NETDT26.10.

A surprise worth knowing: RBKP-ZTERM is empty, and that is standard

After the fix, RBKP-ZTERM was empty while RBKP-ZBD1T and the vendor line BSEG-ZTERM were correct. Before we treated this as a bug, we compared it with invoices posted manually in MIRO on the same system. They looked the same: RBKP-ZTERM empty, RBKP-ZBD1T filled, and the terms key only on the FI vendor line.

This is what we observed on our release. Check it on yours before you write a test case that expects the key in RBKP. Testers should check the vendor line in BSEG, because that is the line the payment run reads.

Choosing the payment terms key when nobody sends one

The business rule, in order:

  1. The key sent by the external system (it must exist in T052, otherwise the message is rejected).
  2. The PO header (EKKO-ZTERM).
  3. The vendor company-code data (LFB1-ZTERM).
  4. Otherwise, the T052 key whose days are closest to dueDate − documentDate. On a tie, take the shorter one.

For step 4 we only consider keys with baseline = document date (ZDART = 'B'), no cash discount, no fixed day, and no day limit. Without that filter, SAP's sample keys (0001…0009, with discounts or other baseline rules) would be picked by accident.

Three more pitfalls from the same project

  1. SELECT … FOR ALL ENTRIES removes duplicate rows. We summed invoiced quantities from EKBE and selected only ebeln, ebelp, zekkn, shkzg, menge. Two invoices with the same quantity on the same account assignment collapsed into one row. The "open quantity" was wrong, and the next invoice was booked on the wrong account assignment line. Always select the full key (gjahr, belnr, buzei) when you aggregate after FAE.
  2. Exchange rate overflow. KURSF is DEC 9,5. If the external system sends the real rate (e.g. 25,437.68 VND per USD) and you move it straight into the field, you get BCD_FIELD_OVERFLOW. Divide by the translation factors in TCURF first (USD→VND 1:1000 gives 25.43768), and catch the overflow as a validation error instead of a dump.
  3. Multiple account assignment with sequential distribution (EKPO-TWRKZ = 1). MIRO fills the account assignment lines one after another. When you pass ACCOUNTINGDATA, the BAPI does not do that for you. We rebuilt the distribution from EKKN and the invoiced quantities per ZEKKN (EKBE), and used MRM_QUANTITY_AMOUNT_DISTRIBUTE for the amount split. Credit memos and subsequent debits/credits are split proportionally instead.

Caveats

  • Both enhancement points and the variables S_RBKPV and F_FIX_PAYMENT_TERMS are internal, unreleased SAP code. Re-test after every upgrade or support package. If a released API (for example the Supplier Invoice OData/SOAP service) meets your requirement, prefer it.
  • If you do not need the terms key on the document, the simplest standard-only option is to send only BLINE_DATE and DSCT_DAYS1, with no key and no enhancement.
  • Make sure your FI team agrees that "key from the PO, days overridden" is the reporting behaviour they want.

Have you solved the "terms key + fixed due date" requirement differently, for example with a BAdI, a substitution, or a released API? Share it in the comments.

entry.title: Scheduling a Report by Email with a Custom Subject and Body in SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
Introduction

Many business teams need a report delivered to their inbox on a fixed schedule rather than logging in to run it manually. In SAP SuccessFactors, this can be achieved using the Report Distributor, which lets you bundle one or more reports, choose recipients, define your own email subject and message, and run the whole thing on a schedule.

In this blog post, I will walk you through the end-to-end steps to schedule a report by email with a customised email subject and body, with screenshots for each step.

Step-by-Step Configuration

Step 1: Open Report Centre and go to View Schedules

Navigate to Report Centre and click View Schedules in the top-right corner of the page.

Report Centre – View Schedules Report Centre – View Schedules

Step 2: Switch to the legacy Report Distributor tool

On the View Schedules page, click Switch to the legacy Report Distributor Tool.

Switch to the legacy Report Distributor ToolSwitch to the legacy Report Distributor Tool

Step 3: Create a new bundle

Click New Bundle and provide the following details:

  • Bundle Name – a meaningful name for your scheduled report.
  • Page Size – for example, LETTER.
  • Export Type / Export Format – the output file type of the attachment (for example PDF or Excel) will depend on the option you select here.

Click OK to create the bundle.

Add New BundleAdd New Bundle

Step 4: Add the report to the bundle

Click on your newly created bundle in the list, then click Add Item and select Add Report.

Select the new bundle and click Add ItemSelect the new bundle and click Add Item
 
Add Item options: Add Report, Add Excel Table, Add CSV TableAdd Item options: Add Report, Add Excel Table, Add CSV Table

In the report tree, expand All reports not in this bundle and select ReportCenter (or any other section) to find your report.

Expand All reports not in this bundle and select ReportCenterExpand All reports not in this bundle and select ReportCenter

Select the required report and click Add. The report is now added to the bundle.

Choose the report from the listChoose the report from the list
 
The report now appears in the bundle’s Item ListThe report now appears in the bundle’s Item List

Step 5: Add recipients

Open the Recipients tab, click Add Recipients, search for the user(s) who should receive the email, select them and click Add.

 Search for and add the recipients

Step 6: Customise the email (Edit E-mail)

Click the bundle name, then select File from the menu at the top left and choose Edit E-mail.

File > Edit E-mail

By default, the Default message option is selected. To use your own content, select the Override for <Bundle Name> option. You can also add localisations for the languages enabled in your system by using the language selector.

Override option and language (localisation) selector

Enter the From Address Prefix, the Subject for E-mail and the Body of message. You can personalise the content using these tokens:

  • [%USERNAME%]
  • [%FULLNAME%]
  • [%EMAIL%]
 Custom email subject and body using tokens

Once done, click Submit.

Step 7: Schedule the report

Go to the Schedule tab and click Add.

Schedule tab – Add

Enter the start date, start time and how often the schedule should recur (One Time, Daily, Weekly or Monthly), then click OK. The schedule is added and the report is now scheduled.

Scheduler – start date, time and frequency

 

Result

At the scheduled date and time, the recipients receive an email with your custom subject and message, with the report attached in the export format you selected when creating the bundle.

 

Email received by the recipient with the report attached

Conclusion

Using the Report Distributor, you can automate report delivery with a personalised email and a recurring schedule, saving users from running reports manually. I hope this post helps you set up scheduled report emails in your own system. Feel free to share your questions or experiences in the comments.

entry.title: SAP Document and Reporting Compliance: e-Invoice in Convergent Invoice using Extensibility
entry.content:
You want to enable your system to create electronic documents for invoices posted via Convergent Invoice using SAP Document and Reporting Compliance. In this blog, we'll show you an example of how this can be achieved using extensibility, with Belgium (BE) as a reference country. 

Before you begin, ensure that the Financial Accounting Document, Sales and Distribution Billing Document e-Invoicing option is already available in your system for the specific country, including the eDocument customization and eDocument process. An implementation overview note (ex: For BE refer this note https://me.sap.com/notes/2424886. ) will be available for each country e-Invoicing process if the country is localized by SAP for Financial Accounting Document, Sales and Distribution Billing Document.  If you need to set up e-Invoicing from scratch for your country without an existing Financial Accounting Document, Sales and Distribution Billing Document localization, refer to the Extensibility for Electronic Document Processing in Private Cloud

Implement the following SAP Note before proceeding:

  • 3052578 — this note contains the list of relevant prerequisite notes to enable e-invoice for Convergent Invoice

Steps to Create Electronic Documents

1. Configure the eDocument Type Table

entry.title: The SAP B1 Barcode Gap: Why a Missing Label at Goods Receipt Is a Supply Chain Problem - Part 1
entry.content:
The gap nobody writes a requirement for

A truck backs into the dock. Inventory is unloaded, someone posts a Goods Receipt PO in SAP Business One, and the stock enters the system. Everyone moves on.

A week later, a picker finds an item in a bin with a handwritten sticker and wonders whether it belongs to the lot under quality hold.

I saw this at an SAP Business One project using bin-managed warehouses and batch-tracked materials. Receiving and master data were clean; the gap was between the posted GRPO and the physical item.

SAP Business One doesn’t print inventory barcode labels. You can print the GRPO document, but there’s no built-in way to print labels for an item from a specific receipt, lot, and bin. The feature simply isn’t included. "We need labels” often gets filed as a nice-to-have, then sits in the backlog for two years.

Receiving is where physical stock becomes data

Everything downstream in a warehouse is a copy of a decision made at receiving.

The bin balance is a copy. The cycle count variance is a copy. The pick confirmation, the lot, the certificate of analysis you hand a customer two years later during an audit. All tracing back to the moment someone decided this box is this item, this lot, this bin.

When that decision lives only in a posted document and not on the item, you have created a translation step. Somebody has to re-derive it later, from memory, from a packing slip, or from a sticker written in marker. Translation steps show up in two very different ways.

The daily cost: operational efficiency

  • Put-away drifts. Unlabelled stock goes to the nearest open bin rather than the assigned one. The system says one thing, the rack says another, and the gap widens quietly.
  • Picking slows. Two lots of the same item in adjacent bins are indistinguishable without a label. The picker either guesses or goes and asks someone.
  • Cycle counts stretch. Counters spend their time identifying material instead of counting it.

This appears as a warehouse that feels slower than it should and overtime nobody can attribute to anything in particular. That is usually what operational inefficiency looks like from the inside.

The rare cost: supply chain resilience

If lot traceability depends on paperwork and people's memory, then a supplier defect or a customer recall turns into an archaeology project. The question which customers received material from this lot always has an answer. What is in doubt is whether you can produce it in two hours or two weeks.

And this is where it stops being a warehouse issue. This client is a supplier: their material ends up inside somebody else's product. When they cannot trace a lot quickly, their customer cannot either, and nor can the customer after that. The weakness does not stay put. It propagates up every tier that depends on them.

Why this lands harder on SMBs

A large manufacturer solves this without thinking about it. They have a WMS layer, or dedicated label management software, or an integration team that will build a service. The gap exists for them too, they just have budgeted ways to close it.

Small and mid-sized businesses are running SAP Business One precisely because they do not have those options. The ERP is the stack. There is no middleware tier, usually no internal developer. So the gap stays open. The workaround becomes the process, the process becomes the culture.

What I built

I closed the gap with three things: Crystal Reports, the Boyum B1 Usability Package, and a Zebra label printer. No custom code, and no new software vendor.

From a posted GRPO, a user now clicks one button, selects the item, the bin and the lot, says how many copies, and the labels come out. 

The output. Item code top left, lot number top right, bin location in large type, a barcode of the item code, and the description along the bottom. Everything a picker needs, printed at the moment the stock lands.

The material is now identified where it sits instead of depending on who remembers what. Lot and bin are captured on the item at the moment of receipt, which turns the recall question from a filing-cabinet problem into a query.

Conclusion

Receiving turns physical stock into data. Missing labels compromise put-away accuracy and picking speed every day, and traceability when a quality hold or recall occurs.
Small and mid-sized manufacturers bear the cost, not through negligence, but because standard fixes require budgets, middleware, or developers they lack.
What’s encouraging is how little it took to close the gap: three tools, no custom code, and a solution the client's next consultant can maintain.

What's next in this series

  • Part 2 — Build, buy, or configure. The decision framework I used, why configuring an owned toolset beat adding a vendor, and the solution architecture.
  • Part 3 — What actually broke. Nine real failures, including the one that forced a redesign and the one that exposed a wrong assumption in my own data model.
  • Part 4 — The reusable pattern. Where this generalizes, what it does not solve, and why SME ERP maturity is a supply chain resilience question rather than an IT one.

If you have solved this differently, an SAP B1 add-on, a dedicated label engine, a ZPL-over-raw-socket approach, I would like to hear it in the comments. There is more than one right answer here, and the client's constraints shaped mine.

entry.title: Building an MCP Server with SAP CAP on SAP BTP: AI Assistant for SAP S/4HANA (Part 1 of 2)
entry.content:
Introduction

An earlier post, Connecting SAP S/4HANA to AI with MCP and SAP BTP, described a small MCP server in Python that let an AI assistant read SAP S/4HANA data through OData. The approach worked, but every part of it was custom code: a custom login check, custom logging and a custom deployment.

This two-part series rebuilds the same assistant the SAP way, with the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) on SAP BTP. The result is one CAP application that answers questions about SAP S/4HANA data, both through an MCP endpoint for AI tools and through standard OData.

  • Part 1 (this post): the architecture, the CAP project file by file, connecting to S/4HANA, the MCP endpoint, login with the user's own token, and deployment.
  • Part 2: securing the application and adding AI-powered SAP Basis monitoring over RFC.

This post is for SAP Basis, BTP and integration people who know S/4HANA and want a working pattern for connecting AI to it. Full-time development experience is not required; the places where SAP Basis knowledge matters are highlighted along the way.

Why SAP CAP instead of a hand-written MCP server

CAP provides, out of the box, the capabilities that previously had to be built by hand, in a form that other SAP teams recognise and can support.

Topic Hand-written Python server SAP CAP application

LoginCustom API key checkXSUAA login and roles, checked by CAP for every request
Who may do whatOne key for everyoneRole collections in the BTP cockpit, e.g. User
Connecting to S/4HANACustom HTTP calls and credentialsCAP remote services through a BTP destination and the Cloud Connector
Audit trailPrint statements@cap-js/audit-logging, SAP's standard plugin (Part 2)
Personal dataNot described@PersonalData annotations in the CDS model
Deploymentcf push per appOne MTA archive: mbt build and cf deploy

The tools themselves stay almost the same. The difference is everything around them: login, roles, connectivity, logging and deployment now follow the SAP standard.

Architecture

Users only ever open the approuter. It handles the login and passes the user's token to the chat website, which calls the CAP app with that same token. The CAP app reaches S/4HANA through the BTP destination and the Cloud Connector. Nothing stores business data on the way.

Prerequisites

  • SAP BTP subaccount with Cloud Foundry enabled, and entitlements for Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA), Destination and Connectivity.
  • SAP Cloud Connector connected to the subaccount, exposing the S/4HANA Gateway (/sap/opu/odata/).
  • A BTP destination of type HTTP to S/4HANA through the Cloud Connector (ProxyType: OnPremise).
  • SAP S/4HANA with the standard OData APIs activated in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, e.g. API_BUSINESS_PARTNER and API_SALES_ORDER_SRV.
  • A technical SAP user for the destination. Read-only authorizations only; more on this in Part 2.
  • On your laptop: Node.js 22, @SAP/cds-dk (npm i -g @SAP/cds-dk), the Cloud MTA Build Tool (npm i -g mbt) and the Cloud Foundry CLI with the MultiApps plugin.

The project, file by file

The project is created with cds init and keeps CAP's standard layout. The following files make it a CAP project and are the best starting point:

sap-ai-assistant-cap/
├─ package.json          CAP dependencies and the cds configuration (remote services, auth, audit log)
├─ srv/
│  ├─ s4-service.cds     the service: entities and one function per tool, @requires: 'User'
│  ├─ s4-service.js      the handlers behind those functions
│  ├─ external/          imported SAP API definitions (cds import)
│  ├─ server.js          start-up: destination, MCP endpoint
│  ├─ mcp.js             the MCP endpoint /mcp
│  └─ sap/               the tools, the allow-list of SAP APIs, metadata reading
├─ app/
│  ├─ router/            the approuter: the only address users open (login)
│  └─ web/               the chat website
├─ xs-security.json      scopes and role collections
└─ mta.yaml              how everything is built and deployed together

The three that matter most:

  • srv/s4-service.cds declares the service: who may use it, and which functions it offers.
  • package.json, in its cds section, declares where SAP is, how login works and where audit entries go. It's configuration, not code.
  • mta.yaml puts the CAP app, the website and the approuter into one deployable archive, together with the BTP services they need.

A quick way to tell a CAP project from "Node.js code that calls SAP" is cds watch. It starts the whole service locally, with mocked login, from these files alone.

Connecting CAP to SAP S/4HANA

CAP reaches S/4HANA through a remote service that points at the BTP destination. No URL, user or password is in the code; the destination and the Cloud Connector handle all of that.

First, import the API definition of the Business Partner API (the EDMX from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub):

cds import API_BUSINESS_PARTNER.edmx --as cds

Then declare the remote services in package.json. The destination name is set at deployment, not in the code:

"cds": {
  "requires": {
    "API_BUSINESS_PARTNER": { "kind": "odata-v2", "model": "srv/external/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER" },
    "S4HANA": { "kind": "odata-v2", "credentials": { "path": "/sap/opu/odata" } }
  }
}

In srv/server.js, every remote service gets the destination from an environment variable that mta.yaml fills in:

const destination = process.env.SAP_DESTINATION
for (const conf of Object.values(cds.env.requires)) {
  if (conf?.kind === 'odata-v2') conf.credentials = { ...conf.credentials, destination }
}

The application uses two styles of access:

  • Typed CDS queries on imported APIs, e.g. a projection on A_BusinessPartner. CAP translates OData V4 options such as $filter and $select into the V2 call automatically.
  • Raw OData V2 calls for everything else: await s4.send({ method: 'GET', path: 'sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV/A_SalesOrder?$top=5' }). This lets the tools work with any allowed API without importing each one.

Two Basis details to check before investigating the code:

  1. Cloud Connector resource: the path /sap/opu/odata/ must be exposed, with "path and all sub-paths".
  2. The services must be active in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE. A service that isn't answers with a 403 or 404 that looks like an authorization problem.

Tools as CAP functions, and the MCP endpoint

Every tool exists once and is offered through two doors: as a CAP function over OData, and as an MCP tool at /mcp. Both give exactly the same answer text, because both call the same JavaScript function.

The service in srv/s4-service.cds:

@requires: 'User'
@path    : '/odata/v4/s4'
service S4Service {

  @readonly
  entity BusinessPartners as projection on bp.A_BusinessPartner {
    key BusinessPartner, BusinessPartnerFullName as Name, CreationDate
  };

  function list_sap_services(search : String)                           returns LargeString;
  function query_sap(![service] : String, entity_set : String,
                     ![filter] : String, ![select] : String, top : Integer) returns LargeString;
  function find_sap_data(question : String, top : Integer)               returns LargeString;
  function search_business_partners(name : String, top : Integer)       returns LargeString;
  function get_sales_order(sales_order : String)                         returns LargeString;
  // ... one function per tool
}

@requires: 'User' is the whole authorization check for the OData door. CAP refuses any request without a valid login (401) or without the User role (403) before any application code runs. @readonlyand the absence of any create/update function make the service read-only by design.

The MCP endpoint is a small Express route in srv/mcp.js, using the official SDK @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. It sits behind CAP's own login middleware, so the same check applies:

app.post('/mcp', ...cds.middlewares.before, requireUser,
         express.json({ limit: '1mb' }), handle)

handle creates a stateless MCP server for each request. It lists the tools (each marked readOnlyHint: true) and runs a tool by calling the same function the OData door uses. Being stateless means several app instances can serve the same chat without shared sessions.

For /mcp, cds.middlewares.before is the key line: it gives a custom route the same login, user context and audit hooks as CAP's own services.

Answering plain-English questions from SAP's own metadata

Fixed tools only answer the questions that were anticipated at design time. To go further, the assistant gets four general tools:

Tool What it does

list_sap_servicesLists the SAP APIs the assistant may use: an allow-list, cross-checked against the services that are really registered in the system (/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE)
describe_sap_serviceReads an API's $metadata: its entity sets, fields with their SAP labels, and links
query_sapReads rows with $filter, $select, $orderby and $top, with a hard limit on rows and answer size
find_sap_dataTakes one plain-English question and works out the service, entity set and filters itself

find_sap_data is the most powerful of the four. It reads every allowed service's $metadata (cached for an hour) and scores each entity set against the words in the question. It uses SAP's own descriptions and field labels, so "how many sales orders were created last month" finds A_SalesOrder and CreationDate without a single hardcoded mapping. The answer always states exactly what it queried, so a user can check it.

The project follows a strict rule: no company data, sample IDs or hardcoded values in the code. Every number, name and ID in an answer comes from SAP at the moment of the question. Adding a new standard API is a configuration change (SAP_EXTRA_SERVICES), not a code change.

Login and roles: the user's own token, no shared key

The biggest change from the Python version: there is no shared API key any more. Every request carries the signed-in user's own login token.

  1. The user opens the approuter address, the only address users ever open. The approuter sends them to the login page of the subaccount's identity provider.
  2. After login, the approuter passes the user's XSUAA token on to the chat website (forwardAuthToken: true).
  3. The website calls the CAP app's /mcp with that same token.
  4. CAP checks the token and the User role on every request, for OData and MCP alike.

The roles are defined in xs-security.json:

{
  "scopes": [{ "name": "$XSAPPNAME.User", "description": "Use the SAP assistant" }],
  "role-templates": [{ "name": "User", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.User"] }],
  "role-collections": [{
    "name": "SAP AI Assistant CAP User",
    "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.User"]
  }]
}

An administrator assigns the role collection to users in the BTP cockpit (Security → Users). Because the token belongs to a person, CAP knows who asked what, which the audit log in Part 2 builds on.

In mta.yaml, the login service's redirect-uris are also restricted to the approuter's own address. As a result, no other app on the shared cfapps domain can receive a login result meant for this one.

Important: once a role collection is assigned to users, you can't add roles to it through xs-security.json. The XSUAA service update fails with "Adding role-template-references to role collection ... is restricted". Create a new role collection with a new name instead.

Build and deploy

Everything goes to Cloud Foundry as one MTA archive. mta.yaml describes three apps and the services they use:

Module What it is Binds

...-srvThe CAP app: OData and /mcpXSUAA, Destination, Connectivity
...-webThe chat websiteXSUAA
...-routerThe approuter, the only address users openXSUAA

System-specific values are kept out of git in a small extension file, config.mtaext:

_schema-version: '3.1'
ID: sap-ai-assistant-cap.config
extends: sap-ai-assistant-cap
parameters:
  sap-destination: <your BTP destination name>
  router-host: <the host name users open>

Then build and deploy:

npm ci
mbt build
cf deploy mta_archives/sap-ai-assistant-cap_1.0.0.mtar -e config.mtaext

Finally, assign the role collection to the users in the BTP cockpit.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them:

  1. Build timeout. On a laptop, the website's build took longer than mbt's default 10 minutes, so an old archive was deployed without any warning. Fix: build-parameters: timeout: 40m on that module.
  2. Stack deprecation. Cloud Foundry warned that cflinuxfs4 is deprecated. Fix: stack: cflinuxfs5 on each module, then rebuild and redeploy (a restage alone doesn't change it).
  3. Role collections are frozen once assigned. See the login section: create a new collection rather than changing an assigned one.
  4. Duplicate downloads. When a new version of the project zip is downloaded, the browser may save it as ... (1).zip, and the old archive is easily unpacked by mistake. A quick Select-String for a new line of code before mbt build saves a lot of confusion.

The result

Users open one address, log in with their normal company account, and ask questions about SAP S/4HANA data in plain English. Every answer is read live from SAP at the moment of the question.

Key points for SAP Basis consultants:

  • One login, checked twice. The website checks the token, and the CAP app checks it again for every request. Someone who finds the CAP app's own address still can't get in without a valid token and the role.
  • Nothing stored. There's no database; every answer comes from SAP when it's asked, so there's no copy of business data in BTP.
  • Read-only by design. The service has no write functions and its entities are @readonly.

Conclusion and what's next

Rebuilding the MCP server with SAP CAP took more thought than writing a Python script, but the result is something an SAP team can own:

  • standard login and roles;
  • connectivity through the destination and the Cloud Connector;
  • one deployable archive.

The AI side, the MCP endpoint, turned out to be the smallest part. Doing it properly on BTP was the real work.

Part 2 covers what it takes to make the application safe to put in front of real users:

  • a line-by-line security review of the code, including a text pattern that could freeze the app;
  • data rules for the SAP APIs, request limits and the SAP audit log;
  • AI-powered SAP Basis monitoring over RFC, with a dashboard for SM51, SM04, SM58 and SM37.

Thanks for reading. If you've built something similar with CAP and MCP, or have questions about any of the steps, feel free to share your experience in the comments.
