entry.title: "Is there a CDS view for that table?" Answered in SAP Datasphere, no S/4HANA user needed
entry.content:
The situation (you have probably been here)

SAP Datasphere is up and running. The connection to SAP S/4HANA is green. The first replication flow is happily moving data. Everything is perfect, except for one small detail: your own S/4HANA user. It has been "requested". The ticket has been "in progress" for three weeks. It has seen more status changes than some of your sales orders. 🙃

And of course, this is exactly the moment someone asks: "We need table X with columns A, B and C. Is there a CDS view we can replicate? Ideally with delta?"

Without an S/4HANA user you have no SE11 where-used list, no ADT and no View Browser. What you do have is the source browser of the replication flow, which searches names and descriptions. It cannot tell you which columns a view contains. It also keeps quiet about filters a view applies. That leaves you with educated guessing, or with asking a colleague at the customer for screenshots, again.

In my case the table was BUT050 (business partner relationships). Instead of guessing, I built a small metadata model that only needs the Datasphere connection that is already there. It has since become a self-service tool for the developers on the project.

What already exists

Credit where it is due. There are good tools for this question:

  • In the S/4HANA system: the where-used list in SE11, the SQL Dependency Analyzer in ADT, the View Browser app, or SE16 on DD26S plus DDLDEPENDENCY. All of them need an S/4HANA user.
  • I_DataExtractionEnabledView (SQL view IXTRCTNENBLDVW, available since S/4HANA 2020) lists the CDS views that are enabled for extraction. See CDS Views Enabled for Data Extraction and KBA 3472575.
  • Top-down analysis in Datasphere: McCoy & Partners describe how to replicate the CDS view stack (DDCDS_BOE_VIEWSTACK_INFO_UNION) and resolve the dependencies of a given CDS view in Datasphere: Gaining additional insights into technical details of CDS views.
  • Field-level mapping without any system: the community SAP Table to CDS Mapper (Project Kernseife) maps table fields to CDS elements for a standard S/4HANA 2025 system, including C1 release information.

What I was missing was the bottom-up direction (table → views), answered for the actual system, including custom Z views:

  1. Which CDS views are built on this table, and which of them are extraction-enabled, released and CDC-capable?
  2. Which view column comes from which table field?
  3. Does the view apply a WHERE filter?

The idea: six DDIC objects as remote tables

Everything you need is in the ABAP Dictionary. Datasphere can read it through the S/4HANA on-premise connection as remote tables (container ABAPTABLES). Replicate them as snapshots once a week, for example with a task chain. That is enough, because metadata only changes with transports.

DDIC object Content Used for

DD26SView → base table / base viewView lineage
DD27SView field → base table fieldField lineage
DD28SConditions of a view (WHERE and join conditions)Filters
DDLDEPENDENCYDDL source ↔ CDS entity (OBJECTTYPE = 'STOB') ↔ generated SQL view ('VIEW')Name resolution
DDDDLSRCTDescription of DDL sourcesDescriptions
IXTRCTNENBLDVWSQL view of I_DataExtractionEnabledViewExtraction, release and CDC flags

A detail that surprised me: the ABAPTABLES container does not only offer tables. It also offers the generated SQL views of CDS views. That is how I_DataExtractionEnabledView ends up in Datasphere without a replication flow. In our system each of the six objects replicated in under a minute (5 to 51 seconds).

Option 1: Quick & dirty, one SQL view

If you just want an answer today, a single SQL view does the job. Create it in the space that holds the six remote tables, paste the statement and open the data preview. Change BUT050 in the last line to your table. The second condition keeps CDS views only. Remove it if you also want to see classic DDIC views.

It returns one row per table field and CDS view column, with the CDS view name, its description, the three flags and the view's filter. It follows views up to four levels above the table. Each level is one more UNION ALL block, so extending it is copy and paste.

SELECT l."BaseTable",
	l."BaseField",
	l."Level",
	e."OBJECTNAME" AS "CdsEntity",
	l."SqlView",
	l."CdsField",
	t."DDTEXT" AS "Description",
	CASE WHEN x."DATAEXTRACTIONVIEWNAME" IS NULL THEN '' ELSE 'X' END AS "IsExtractionEnabled",
	x."ISSAPRELEASEDVIEW" AS "IsSapReleased",
	x."DELTACHGDATACAPTUREISSUPPORTED" AS "IsCdcSupported",
	flt."Filter"
FROM (
	SELECT p."BaseTable", p."BaseField", p."SqlView", p."CdsField", MIN(p."Level") AS "Level"
	FROM (
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 1 AS "Level", f1."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f1."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		UNION ALL
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 2 AS "Level", f2."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f2."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f2 ON f2."TABNAME" = f1."VIEWNAME" AND f2."FIELDNAME" = f1."VIEWFIELD" AND f2."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f2."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		UNION ALL
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 3 AS "Level", f3."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f3."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f2 ON f2."TABNAME" = f1."VIEWNAME" AND f2."FIELDNAME" = f1."VIEWFIELD" AND f2."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f2."AS4VERS" = '0000'
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f3 ON f3."TABNAME" = f2."VIEWNAME" AND f3."FIELDNAME" = f2."VIEWFIELD" AND f3."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f3."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		UNION ALL
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 4 AS "Level", f4."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f4."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f2 ON f2."TABNAME" = f1."VIEWNAME" AND f2."FIELDNAME" = f1."VIEWFIELD" AND f2."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f2."AS4VERS" = '0000'
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f3 ON f3."TABNAME" = f2."VIEWNAME" AND f3."FIELDNAME" = f2."VIEWFIELD" AND f3."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f3."AS4VERS" = '0000'
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f4 ON f4."TABNAME" = f3."VIEWNAME" AND f4."FIELDNAME" = f3."VIEWFIELD" AND f4."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f4."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
	) AS p
	GROUP BY p."BaseTable", p."BaseField", p."SqlView", p."CdsField"
) AS l
	LEFT JOIN "DDLDEPENDENCY" AS w ON w."OBJECTNAME" = l."SqlView" AND w."OBJECTTYPE" = 'VIEW' AND w."STATE" = 'A'
	LEFT JOIN "DDLDEPENDENCY" AS e ON e."DDLNAME" = w."DDLNAME" AND e."OBJECTTYPE" = 'STOB' AND e."STATE" = 'A'
	LEFT JOIN "DDDDLSRCT" AS t ON t."DDLNAME" = w."DDLNAME" AND t."DDLANGUAGE" = 'E' AND t."AS4LOCAL" = 'A'
	LEFT JOIN "IXTRCTNENBLDVW" AS x ON UPPER(x."DATAEXTRACTIONVIEWNAME") = e."OBJECTNAME"
	LEFT JOIN (
		SELECT c."CONDNAME", STRING_AGG(TRIM(COALESCE(c."NEGATION", '') || ' ' || c."TABNAME" || '.' || c."FIELDNAME" || ' ' || c."OPERATOR" || ' ' || c."CONSTANTS" || ' ' || COALESCE(c."AND_OR", '')), ' ' ORDER BY c."POSITION") AS "Filter"
		FROM "DD28S" AS c
		WHERE c."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND c."AS4VERS" = '0000' AND COALESCE(c."CONSTANTS", '') NOT LIKE '&$SESSION%'
		GROUP BY c."CONDNAME"
	) AS flt ON flt."CONDNAME" = l."SqlView"
WHERE l."BaseTable" = 'BUT050' AND e."OBJECTNAME" IS NOT NULL

How to read the result:

  • Table → views: look at the distinct CdsEntity values, ideally with IsExtractionEnabled = 'X'.
  • Columns: BaseField is the table field, CdsField the view column. In a replication flow the column shows up in CamelCase (RELATIONSHIPCATEGORY → RelationshipCategory).
  • Filter: the conditions of the view as text. The client condition (CLIENT EQ &$SESSION.CLIENT) that every client-dependent view carries is hidden. Lines starting with JL are join conditions, everything else filters rows.

Filtered on I_BPCONTACT: extraction-enabled, released, CDC-capable, and filtered on RELTYP EQ 'BUR001'. The last row shows a level-2 view (I_BPCONTACTTOFUNCANDDEPT) whose join to BUT051 appears as a JL ... JR ... line.

A word of honesty: this is a quick & dirty solution, not a sustainable architecture. It is one big statement, it checks filters only on the view itself and not on the views further down the path, and anyone who edits it in a hurry will regret it later. For a one-off answer it is perfect. If you want to offer it to a team for the long run, read on.

Option 2: A small layered model

For a permanent self-service tool I split the logic into reusable views. The names below are deliberately neutral, so adapt them to your naming convention.

View Purpose

DDIC_VIEW_EDGEView → base object from DD26S (active version), CDS entity names mapped to SQL view names, CAST helper tables DDDDL*TYPES filtered out
DDIC_VIEW_FIELDView fields with their origin from DD27S
DDIC_VIEW_CONDITIONWHERE and join conditions from DD28S as readable text
CDS_OBJECTDDL source → CDS entity → SQL view
CDS_EXTRACTION_ENABLEDExtraction-enabled views with release and CDC flags (joined via UPPER, see below)
CDS_TABLE_LINEAGETable → CDS view, shortest level, all flags, example path
CDS_FIELD_LINEAGETable field → CDS view field, all flags
CDS_VIEW_FILTERFilters per CDS view

Datasphere SQL views support neither WITH nor recursive queries. The lineage views therefore use the same trick as option 1: an unrolled UNION ALL, where level k is a k-fold self-join of the edge view. Six levels covered every case I looked at:

SELECT e1."BaseName" AS "BaseTable",
	2 AS "Level",
	e2."ViewName" AS "ViewName",
	e1."BaseName" || ' > ' || e1."ViewName" || ' > ' || e2."ViewName" AS "Path"
FROM "DDIC_VIEW_EDGE" AS e1
	INNER JOIN "DDIC_VIEW_EDGE" AS e2 ON e2."BaseNode" = e1."ViewName"

A filter on BaseTable is pushed down into level 1, so a query for one table comes back within seconds, even though the views cover the whole dictionary.

Writing six levels by hand is no fun, so I generate the views with a small Python script. It renders every expression twice, as SQL text and as query CSN, and deploys the views via the Datasphere CLI. One CLI pitfall: a SQL view created via CLI without a query CSN deploys "successfully" but returns no rows.

Walking through BUT050

Step 1: Which views are built on the table, and which are extraction-enabled?

Selected candidates on BUT050. Only I_BPCONTACT is extraction-enabled, released and CDC-capable. I_BPRELATIONSHIP_2 exists, but is not enabled for extraction.

Step 2: Which view contains PARTNER1, PARTNER2 and RELTYP?

Three candidate views deliver the fields. Only I_BPCONTACT is extraction-enabled.

Step 3: Does that view filter rows?

And there is the catch: BUT050.RELTYP EQ 'BUR001'.

So the only extraction-enabled view with all three columns delivers contact person relationships only. Our requirement was a customer-specific relationship category, which this view will never return. Without the model we would have found that out after the first load, most likely as "why are so many relationships missing?".

The result for this case: a custom view on I_BPRELATIONSHIP_2 with @analytics.dataExtraction.enabled: true (and CDC), plus a remote table snapshot on BUT050 until then.

Lessons learned, so you don't have to

  1. Upper and lower case. IXTRCTNENBLDVW returns entity names as written in the DDL source, in CamelCase (I_BPContact). DDLDEPENDENCY, DD26S and DD27S use upper case. Without UPPER() in the join, only views whose DDL name is written in upper case match, and every VDM standard view drops out. The nasty part: the result still looks plausible.
  2. Keep your hands off DDHEADANNO. The CDS header annotation table (with a 1,300-character VALUE column) took down our Data Provisioning Agent twice. After about 6.5 minutes the load failed, and from then on every remote table replication in the tenant reported "data provisioning agent is unavailable" until the agent was reconnected. Two out of two is a big enough sample for me. IXTRCTNENBLDVW already provides the extraction and CDC information in condensed form. Replicate any new dictionary table on its own once before you add it to a task chain.
  3. DD28S does contain CDS filters, plus some noise. For CDS SQL views, DD28S contains the WHERE conditions and, for views with joins, the join conditions (marked JL/JR). Every client-dependent view also has a line CLIENT EQ &$SESSION.CLIENT, which you want to hide. AND_OR belongs at the end of a line, not at the start.
  4. Column names. DD27S.VIEWFIELD is upper case (RELATIONSHIPCATEGORY). In the replication flow the same column is called RelationshipCategory.
  5. Coverage check. In our system IXTRCTNENBLDVW lists 5,146 extraction-enabled views. 4,062 of them have a generated SQL view, and all 4,062 were found in DD26S. The remaining 1,084 are view entities (define view entity) without an SQL view, and those are invisible to DD26S, DD27S and DD28S.

Limitations

  • View entities without an SQL view are missing (see lesson 5). For those, the Kernseife mapper is a good cross-check, and DDCDS_BOE_VIEWSTACK_INFO_UNION might close the gap. I have not tested that yet.
  • Filters are only the conditions stored in the dictionary (WHERE and join conditions). Parameters and DCL authorizations are not covered. A quick count after the first load is still a good idea.
  • Release and system state: tested on one S/4HANA on-premise system. Community posts report that I_DataExtractionEnabledView does not necessarily expose every entry known to ODP. I did not verify that.
  • Authorizations: you do not need your own S/4HANA user, but the technical user behind the Datasphere connection must be allowed to read the dictionary tables.

Conclusion

Six dictionary tables, one SQL view (or a handful, if you like it tidy) and a weekly task chain turn "Is there a CDS view for that?" from a guessing game into a three-minute check. It also works for developers who have no S/4HANA access at all. At our customer it now lives on a Confluence page with copy-and-paste queries. My S/4HANA user did arrive in the end, by the way. I barely needed it for this.

I'm curious which table triggers the question in your project, and whether anyone has combined this with DDCDS_BOE_VIEWSTACK_INFO_UNION to cover view entities as well.

Disclosure: This blog post was written with the support of generative AI. The approach, the SQL and all results shown were built, tested and reviewed by me in a SAP Datasphere and SAP S/4HANA system.

entry.title: Setting Up RTI Cockpit: bgRFC Queue Errors in SAP IBP — A Practical Setup and Configuration Guide
entry.content:
• Introduction
  • Architecture Overview
  • What the App Shows You
  • Prerequisites
  • Step 1: Identify All ERP Systems Participating in RTI Integration
  • Step 2: Prepare the ERP Side
  • Step 3: Update Cloud Connector Resource Mapping (Cloud Connector only)
  • Step 4: Create Communication Arrangements in SAP IBP
  • Step 5: Set Up Authorization in SAP IBP
  • Verification Checklist
  • Conclusion
  • References

Introduction

Managing integration errors between SAP Integrated Business Planning (IBP) and connected ERP systems via Real-Time Integration (RTI) has traditionally meant navigating multiple monitoring transactions — checking background RFC (bgRFC) queues in one place, reviewing application logs in another. The RTI Cockpit: bgRFC Queue Errors app, introduced in SAP IBP 2611, consolidates this into a single screen.

With RTI Cockpit, you can view, filter, and act on bgRFC integration errors from both SAP IBP and all connected SAP ECC or SAP S/4HANA systems without switching tools. Errors can be reprocessed or removed directly from the app.

Early adopter feature: In IBP 2611, RTI Cockpit is available to a limited group of early adopters. To request access for your system, contact SAP using component SCM-IBP-INT-RTI-CPT.

This guide covers the end-to-end setup: ERP-side note installation and user creation, the SAP IBP communication arrangement, and the SAP IBP authorization configuration — including a non-obvious requirement that causes the app to silently show an incomplete error list if missed.

Architecture Overview

RTI Cockpit sits in SAP IBP and retrieves bgRFC error data from both the SAP IBP side and all connected external systems. It also reads from the IBP application log to enrich the error information it displays.

This is why the SAP IBP authorization setup requires two business catalogs, not one — a detail covered in Step 5.

What the App Shows You

Before diving into setup, let's understand how RTI Cockpit: bgRFC Queue Errors displays and how it behaves.

The app consolidates bgRFC integration issues from both SAP IBP and all connected external systems into a single screen. Errors that failed for the same reason are grouped together, allowing you to identify, prioritize, and reprocess faulty units without navigating multiple monitoring transactions.

Note: The app shows a snapshot of integration monitoring data and does not update automatically in real time. Data is collected when the application is opened and when you use Refresh Data. As a result, repeating the same search with identical filter criteria can return different results if integration processing has continued or if other users have performed actions in the meantime.

You can filter the error list by:

FilterDescriptionSortable
Error typeMaster data, Transactional data, ConnectionNo
SystemThe system where the error occurred: SAP IBP or External SystemNo
Planning areaPlanning areas linked to a Real-Time Integration profileYes
External logical systemLogical system of the connected ERP systemYes
SAP IBP logical systemLogical system entries linked to the RTI Profile, representing integration routes from connected on-premise systems (CIF logical system on the ERP side)Yes
DirectionInbound or OutboundNo
Action statusCurrent status of the most recent action triggered from the appNo
Blocked objectsFilter by blocked objectsYes
Faulty unitsFilter by number of faulty unitsNo
Unit created onDate the unit was created in the bgRFC queueYes
Unit last executed onDate the unit was last executed in the bgRFC queueYes

Note on Error type: The error type reflects the data type of the integration process during which the error occurred, not necessarily the root cause. For example, if a transactional data integration fails because required master data is missing, the error is still categorized as Transactional data. Use this filter to prioritize corrective actions, but investigate the detailed error message to identify the actual root cause.

Three actions are available on selected errors:

  • Restart — triggers reprocessing of the selected faulty units in the system where the error occurred. This does not fix the root cause; it only retries the integration. Resolve the underlying issue in SAP IBP or the connected external system before restarting, otherwise the same error will recur.
  • Delete — removes the selected units from the queue. This action is irreversible: deleted units cannot be reprocessed. Use it when a failed unit is no longer relevant or should not be processed further. Note that deleting a unit does not resolve the underlying cause — if the root cause remains, similar errors will occur again after the next integration run.
  • Refresh Data — recollects the latest monitoring data from SAP IBP and all connected external systems. This is different from the standard Go button, which reloads existing records based on filter settings. Use Refresh Data after a Restart or Delete to confirm whether the action completed successfully. Because actions are processed asynchronously, the action status may not update immediately without a refresh.

Note on multi-IBP landscapes: The app can properly monitor errors that originated from the current SAP IBP system or that belong to integration models targeting it. If errors from an external system appear with empty fields for Error Type, Object Type, Planning Area, and SAP IBP Logical System, those errors originated from a different SAP IBP system. This can occur when a single external system is connected to multiple SAP IBP systems — in that case, each IBP system will only display full details for its own errors.

Prerequisites

Before starting, confirm the following:

  • SAP IBP 2611 system with RTI Cockpit activated (early adopter access)
  • Admin access to the connected SAP ECC or SAP S/4HANA system (to install SAP Notes via SNOTE, create users and PFCG roles)
  • SAP IBP administrator access (Communication Arrangements, Communication Systems, Communication Users, Maintain Business Roles, Maintain Business Users)

Step 1: Identify All ERP Systems Participating in RTI Integration

Steps 2, 3, and 4 must be repeated for every external SAP ERP system connected to SAP IBP via Real-Time Integration. Before starting, compile the full list of these systems.

The easiest way to do this in SAP IBP is to review the existing SAP_COM_0684 communication arrangements — there is one per connected ERP system for the standard RTI integration. RTI Cockpit requires an additional SAP_COM_0B50 arrangement for each of these same systems. The existing SAP_COM_0684 arrangements remain in place and are not replaced.

Note down for each system:

  • The system identifier / logical system name
  • The existing SAP_COM_0684 communication system (reused in Step 4)

This list drives all subsequent steps.

Step 2: Prepare the ERP Side

Repeat this step for each ERP system identified in Step 1.

The RTI Cockpit retrieves error data from the ERP system via two RFC function modules. These must be installed and a dedicated technical user must be created before the communication channel can be established from SAP IBP.

2.1 Install SAP Note 3781192

In your SAP ECC or SAP S/4HANA system, install SAP Note 3781192 using transaction SNOTE. This note delivers the RFC function modules used by the cockpit.

After installation, verify that the following function modules exist in the ERP system:

  • CIF_CKPT_GET_ERROR_UNITS_IBP
  • CIF_CKPT_EXECUTE_ACTION_IBP

2.2 Create a Technical Communication User

In transaction SU01, create a new user with User Type = System.

Note for ECC systems: verify the appropriate user type for your ECC release, as user type naming may differ from S/4HANA.

Note down the username and password — you will need them in Step 4.

2.3 Create a PFCG Role and Assign It to the User

In transaction PFCG, create a customer-specific role. On the Authorizations tab, add RFC execution authorization for the two RTI Cockpit function modules:

  • CIF_CKPT_GET_ERROR_UNITS_IBP
  • CIF_CKPT_EXECUTE_ACTION_IBP

Generate the authorization profile, then assign the role to the technical user you created in step 2.2 (via the Users tab → User Comparison → Full Comparison).

Step 3: Update Cloud Connector Resource Mapping (Cloud Connector only)

Repeat this step for each ERP system identified in Step 1.

If your ERP systems are connected to SAP IBP via the SAP Cloud Connector, the two new RFC function modules introduced by SAP Note 3781192 must be explicitly allowed in the Cloud Connector resource mapping for each relevant ERP system connection.

Review the existing resource access control list for each ERP system and ensure the following RFC function modules are permitted:

  • CIF_CKPT_GET_ERROR_UNITS_IBP
  • CIF_CKPT_EXECUTE_ACTION_IBP

Cloud Connector supports two rule types for RFC resource access:

Rule typeHow to configureWhen to use
Exact matchEnter the full RFC function module name (e.g. CIF_CKPT_GET_ERROR_UNITS_IBP)When you want to allow only specific, named function modules
Prefix-basedEnter a prefix followed by * (e.g. CIF_CKPT* or CIF*)When you want to allow all function modules sharing a common naming prefix

If you are using a prefix-based rule, a CIF_CKPT* prefix covers both RTI Cockpit function modules specifically. A broader CIF* prefix covers all CIF-related function modules, which may already be in place for the existing RTI integration.

If the required resource access is not configured here, RTI Cockpit will be unable to call into the affected ERP system — the RFC calls will be blocked at the Cloud Connector before they reach the ERP system.

Note: If the ERP system has multiple application servers and SAP_COM_0684 is configured with load balancing, the RFC function modules must be permitted on every application server entry in the Cloud Connector resource mapping — not just one.

Step 4: Create Communication Arrangements in SAP IBP

A SAP_COM_0B50 communication arrangement must exist for every external SAP ERP system that already has a SAP_COM_0684 arrangement. If SAP_COM_0684 is configured for a given ERP system, RTI Cockpit requires a corresponding SAP_COM_0B50 for that same system.

Reusing the Existing Communication System

If your RTI integration is already running, you likely have communication arrangements for scenario SAP_COM_0684 configured for each ERP connection. The good news is that the same communication system used by SAP_COM_0684 can be reused for SAP_COM_0B50 — you do not need to create a new one from scratch.

For each connected ERP system:

  1. In SAP IBP, open the Communication Systems app. Find and open the communication system used by the SAP_COM_0684 arrangement for that ERP connection.
  2. Switch to edit mode, add the outbound technical user you created in Step 2, and save.
  3. Open the Communication Arrangements app.
  4. Create a new arrangement based on communication scenario SAP_COM_0B50. As a naming convention best practice, use RTI_SAP_COM_0B50_<SYS><CLNT>, where <SYS> is the ERP system ID and <CLNT> is the client number (for example, RTI_SAP_COM_0B50_PRD001).
  5. Select the same communication system you updated in step 1.
  6. Select the outbound technical user you added in step 2.
  7. Maintain the logical system (logsys) of the external ERP system.
  8. Activate the arrangement and confirm the connection test passes before proceeding.

Repeat for each ERP system in your RTI landscape.

Step 5: Set Up Authorization in SAP IBP

To use RTI Cockpit: bgRFC Queue Errors, business users must be assigned an SAP IBP business role with the appropriate authorizations.

Two Business Catalogs Are Required

The SAP IBP business role must include two business catalogs:

Business CatalogCovers
SAP_IBP_BC_RTICKPT_PCRTI Cockpit bgRFC queue errors
SAP_IBP_BC_LOG_PCApplication log access

If you assign only SAP_IBP_BC_RTICKPT_PC, the app will load but may display fewer errors than are actually present in the bgRFC queue monitoring application. The cockpit appears functional while showing an incomplete picture of your integration health.

Access Levels

Create roles according to the access required:

Role WriteRead Value Help
Full accessUnrestrictedUnrestrictedUnrestricted
Read-onlyNo AccessUnrestrictedUnrestricted

Setup Steps

  1. Open the Maintain Business Roles app in SAP IBP.
  2. Create a new role, enter the Business Role ID and description, and click Create.
  3. Navigate to the Business Catalogs tab and click Add.
  4. Search for RTI, select RTI Cockpit BGRFC Queue Errors (SAP_IBP_BC_RTICKPT_PC), and confirm.
  5. Add a second catalog: search for SAP_IBP_BC_LOG_PC and add it.
  6. For each catalog entry, click Maintain Restrictions and set the access categories according to the table above.
  7. Save the role.
  8. Repeat for each role variant needed (full access, read-only).

Assign Roles to Business Users

  1. Open the Maintain Business Users app.
  2. For each user, navigate to the Assigned Business Roles tab, click Add, select the appropriate role, and save.

Verification Checklist

Use this before handing over to the team:

ERP side (repeat for each system from Step 1)

  •  List of all ERP systems participating in RTI integration compiled
  •  SAP Note 3781192 installed
  •  Function modules CIF_CKPT_GET_ERROR_UNITS_IBP and CIF_CKPT_EXECUTE_ACTION_IBP exist
  •  Technical System user created in SU01
  •  PFCG role with RFC execution for both function modules created and assigned

Cloud Connector (repeat for each ERP system connection)

  •  CIF_CKPT_GET_ERROR_UNITS_IBP added to resource access control list
  •  CIF_CKPT_EXECUTE_ACTION_IBP added to resource access control list

SAP IBP side (repeat per ERP system where applicable)

  •  SAP_COM_0B50 communication arrangement created and active for each connected ERP system, connection tests passed
  •  Business roles created with both SAP_IBP_BC_RTICKPT_PC and SAP_IBP_BC_LOG_PC
  •  Roles assigned to business users
  •  Confirmed that the cockpit displays errors consistently with the bgRFC queue monitoring application

Conclusion

The RTI Cockpit in SAP IBP 2611 addresses a practical pain point: integration error monitoring that previously required multiple tools is now available in a single application, with filtering, grouping, and direct action capabilities.

The setup is straightforward, with three points worth emphasizing:

  • The ERP-side PFCG role only needs RFC execution authorization for the two RTI Cockpit function modules — nothing beyond that is required.
  • A SAP_COM_0B50 communication arrangement must be created for every ERP system that already has a SAP_COM_0684 arrangement — if one is missing, RTI Cockpit has no visibility into that system. If SAP_COM_0684 is already in place, you can reuse the same communication system; only the outbound user needs to be added.
  • The SAP IBP business role must include both SAP_IBP_BC_RTICKPT_PC and SAP_IBP_BC_LOG_PC: assigning only the first may result in fewer errors being displayed than actually exist in the bgRFC queue monitoring application.

For early adopter access in SAP IBP 2611, contact SAP via component SCM-IBP-INT-RTI-CPT.

References

  • SAP Help Portal: RTI Cockpit: bgRFC Queue Errors
  • SAP Note 3781192 (install in ECC/S/4HANA)

entry.title: From Knowing to Doing: Acting on Your Side of the SAP BTP Shared Responsibility Model
entry.content:
In my previous blog, Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model on SAP BTP: Who Owns What?, I walked through the fundamental principle that governs cloud security on SAP BTP: SAP secures the platform, but you - the customer - own everything you build and configure on top of it. Identity management, role assignments, secure configuration, audit logging, application security: that's your side of the line.

But understanding who owns what is only half the equation. The harder question is: once you know it's your responsibility, where do you start? This blog answers that question.

What the SAP BTP Security Recommendations Actually Are

Think of this page as the operational counterpart to the Shared Responsibility Model. Where the shared responsibility model tells you what you own, the Security Recommendations tell you how to secure what you own - one service, one configuration setting, one control at a time.

It is a continuously maintained, structured table with a recommendation for each BTP service component in scope. Each row contains:

 

Field

What It Tells You

Component

The BTP service the recommendation applies to

Priority

Critical (address immediately) or Recommended (significantly reduces attack surface)

Secure Operations Map

The security domain it falls under (Authentication & SSO, Data Protection, Network Security, etc.)

Default Setting or Behavior

What SAP ships out of the box - often a sensible default for trial, not for production

Recommendation

The specific hardened configuration you should apply

Index

A unique identifier (e.g., BTP-IAS-0001) for tracking in your compliance tooling

That Index field is more important than it looks. It makes these recommendations traceable - you can reference them in risk registers, remediation plans, and SAP Cloud ALM without ambiguity. More on that below.

Priority Areas: Where the Risk Is Highest

 

1. Identity Authentication Service (IAS): Your Front Door

The Identity Authentication service is the gateway to your entire BTP landscape. It also carries the highest concentration of Critical priority recommendations - which tells you something about how much exposure the wrong configuration creates here.

What to act on first:

  • Protect the administration console with MFA. The default authentication method is username and password - a configuration that is unacceptable for any productive environment. Multifactor authentication must be enforced for all administrator access.
  • Disable self-registration and social sign-on. Unless there is an explicit business case, both should remain disabled to prevent unauthorized account creation and reduce the attack surface on your tenant.
  • Manage obsolete administrators. Dormant accounts with admin privileges are a persistent risk. Regular reviews and automated offboarding are essential.
  • Define and enforce a custom password policy. Relying on default password policies is a compliance gap in most regulatory frameworks.
  • Connect to your corporate identity provider via IAS as a proxy. SAP strongly recommends that IAS acts as the single IdP for BTP, with your corporate IdP connected through it - not directly trusted. This ensures consistent policy enforcement and simplifies governance across multi-IdP landscapes.
  • Enable and regularly review audit logs. The Audit Log Viewer service must be subscribed to and actively monitored. Without it, you have no record of administrative changes or authentication events in your IAS tenant.

2. Authorization and Trust Management : The Privilege Layer 

Once a user is authenticated, Authorization and Trust Management governs what they are allowed to do. The security recommendations for this service are focused on reducing privilege and maintaining integrity of your authorization model over time.

 Key actions:

  • Use custom identity providers. Avoid over-reliance on the default SAP ID service (accounts.sap.com) in productive landscapes. Custom IdPs give you greater control over user lifecycle, policy enforcement, and integration with your corporate directory.
  • Synchronize user data via an identity provisioning service. Manual user management does not scale and introduces inconsistency. Identity Provisioning automates the lifecycle of identities across your connected systems.
  • Control token validity and signing key rotation. Long-lived access tokens and stale signing keys are attacking surface. Define explicit validity periods and establish a rotation schedule for signing keys.
  • Review role collection assignments regularly. Role collections with broad access should be subject to periodic access reviews. Define a least-privilege principle at design time and enforce it operationally. Broad platform roles assigned to large groups of users is a common finding - and a common risk.
  • Monitor and restrict REST API access. Authorization and Trust Management exposes APIs for managing trust and authorization. Access to these APIs should be explicitly scoped and monitored.

3. Connectivity and the Cloud Connector : The On-Premises Bridge 

The Cloud Connector occupies a uniquely sensitive position in any hybrid SAP BTP landscape. It is the component that creates a tunnel between your on-premises systems and the cloud - and it sits physically on your infrastructure, which means it also falls under your side of the shared responsibility line.

What SAP's recommendations require:

  • Restrict OS-level access. This is a Critical recommendation. The server or virtual machine hosting the Cloud Connector should be accessible only to the specific administrators responsible for managing it. Broad OS access in a shared server environment is a direct path to credential theft or service manipulation.
  • Enforce strong password policies on the Cloud Connector itself. The Cloud Connector has its own administration interface with its own credentials. These must not be left at default values.
  • Enable audit logging on the Cloud Connector. Log all administrative actions and access requests. This is foundational for forensic investigation and compliance.
  • Restrict the list of trusted BTP subaccounts. Only subaccounts that have a documented, approved need for on-premises connectivity should be trusted by the Cloud Connector. Over-permissive trust configurations are one of the most common findings in BTP security reviews, and one of the easiest to overlook because the default tends toward convenience.
  • Always use HTTPS for all connection and destination configurations. Insecure protocols in Destination configuration or Identity Provisioning connections have no place in a productive environment. Never disable certificate validation - the Trust All setting exists to solve connectivity issues in development; it must never reach production.
  • Apply TLS certificate lifecycle management. Define explicit processes for certificate renewal, rotation, and revocation. An expired certificate on a critical connectivity path is an availability risk as well as a security risk.

4. Application Security : Built It In, Don't Bolt It On

For organizations building custom applications on BTP, the security recommendations reinforce a principle that experienced developers know but delivery timelines frequently compromise.

Practical guidance:

  • Use BTP's native security features - including protection from common web attacks - as the baseline, not an afterthought.
  • Configure application-based security artifacts (roles, scopes, and authorizations) as part of the development lifecycle and assign them through the cockpit rather than ad hoc.
  • Secure all APIs and interfaces explicitly, including OAuth 2.0 protected resources and principal propagation scenarios.

 

A Practical Starting Point

If you are looking at this list and wondering where to begin, here is a prioritized approach:

  1. Start with Critical items only. Filter the recommendations table for Priority = Critical and treat these as your mandatory baseline - not optional hardening. These are the gaps with the highest likelihood and highest impact of exploitation.
  2. Assign ownership. Each recommendation touches a specific BTP service and a specific operational team. Accountability must be assigned before remediation can begin.
  3. Use the Index for traceability. Reference the BTP-XXX-XXXX identifiers in your risk register and remediation tracking. This creates a clean audit trail and avoids ambiguity when different teams work on findings independently.
  4. Schedule quarterly reviews. SAP updates this page regularly as new services and new risk findings emerge. A static, one-time review is not sufficient. Build this into your security governance calendar.
  5. Connect it to Cloud ALM. If you are operating at scale, implement the Cloud ALM integration to shift from periodic checks to continuous monitoring.

🔖Further Reading:

  • Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model on SAP BTP: Who Owns What? (previous blog in this series)
  • SAP BTP Security Recommendations – SAP Help Portal
  • Explore SAP BTP Security Recommendations: A Hands-On Guide – SAP Community
  • Monitor Security Recommendations with SAP Cloud ALM
  • Setting Up Authentication – SAP BTP Best Practices Guide

🔗Stay connected

entry.title: Your MCP server is open for contributions, but do your users and their agents know about it?
entry.content:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are essential building blocks in agentic engineering scenarios. The MCP protocol is used in the architecture of AI-native or AI-enabled software solutions, and also by the developers building and maintaining said solutions.

What happens though, when the MCP server is not working as expected? What if a feature is missing? Can the MCP client, usually an agent harness, guide its user into finding support and/or feedback channels, or even the contribution guidelines of the project behind the server, when it is open source / InnerSource? Can it contribute bug fixes or missing features? The answer is: No, unless the server is prepared for that.

In this blog post you will find the results of an experiment with a demo MCP server created to show a proof-of-concept for enabling such MCP server "introspection" scenarios, learn how the server works, and get access to the source code to try it yourself!

Why is this important? Open Source and InnerSource User Experience

Here is a topic that I think we in the open source and InnerSource communities don't discuss enough.

I recall my first contribution to an InnerSource project at SAP. It was an internal multi-purpose dashboard called Bridge. This was back when GitHub was still a novelty at SAP and ABAP was king (long live ABAP, seriously!).

Even with the nice experience I had, with the apps available on this dashboard, some features were still missing. What to do from here? Report a missing feature and wait? Can I even find how to do that, without digging too much?

Well, this particular internal tool had something I had only seen so far in (some) open source projects: a clear invitation to contribute, directly found in the tool's user interface.

Reverse mockup of the user interface (UI) of Bridge, created with Copilot Chat - an invitation to contribute is easily found directly on the UI

The journey from user to contributor could be taken directly from the tool, in other words, InnerSource was part of the user experience, not just something hidden behind the scenes, or revealed only to those persistent enough to dig up the source code repository.

The idea of representing open source and InnerSource use cases as part of the user experience of a software solution, or user-facing content, is not entirely new. Nevertheless, the concept does not even have a name yet (to my best knowledge), so I'll coin here the twin terms: Open Source User Experience and InnerSource User Experience.

Such use cases, some of which are not exclusive to open source and / or InnerSource, include:

  • discovering where to ask questions or discuss the software with the project team, other users or interested parties,
  • discovering how to provide feedback, report issues or request new features,
  • and, of course, discovering how to access the source code and perhaps eventually contribute back to it.

This topic is not without "prior art", you can refer to Contributor Personas & Pathways and Contributor Journey Optimization, but it is definitely not explored as much as it should be.

In the example I described above, we saw InnerSource User Experience in action for a "traditional" web application user interface, but how could this be applied to an "AI Native" user interface, such as a user interacting with a remote service through an agent harness (e.g., the Joule Work desktop app, or Claude Code)?

This is what we will explore next.

The "testbed" MCP server

Our open source / InnerSource user experience experiment will need a real-world-like MCP server to serve as a testbed.

I've chosen a use case that is close to my home turf and implemented, with the help of some invisible robots, an MCP server that enables clients to access a catalog of InnerSource projects. This use case is inspired by the InnerSource Pattern "InnerSource (Projects) Portal".

To cater to the use case of listing InnerSource projects, our MCP server will offer a single tool, "list-innersource-projects". It brings a list of fictitious projects containing, for each entry: project name, description, links to source code repository,  support channels and contribution guidelines, and finally, the number of forks.

Let's see how this looks like in action, testing it on the Joule Work desktop app:

Screenshot of Joule Work desktop app listing InnerSource projects

It does not contain the number of stars. This is, on purpose, a missing feature.

The challenge: Taking users where they need to go, when things go wrong

So let's see what happens when I tell my agent to "sort the projects by number of stars":

"Tinkering, blooping, buying RAM..., done: The InnerSource projects data doesn't include a star count — the only popularity metric available is forks. The API also only supports sorting by name or forks.

Would you like me to sort the list by forks instead?"

Note that while I'm showing results in this post using the Joule Work desktop app as an agent harness and MCP client, I also tested it with Claude Code, and I expect to have similar results with other combinations of harnesses and models.

Now, from here, many users would simply say "what a bummer" and move on with their lives without their desired sorting. Users with a continuous improvement mindset may start asking the agent stuff like: "report sorting by stars as a feature" or "where can I give feedback?"; while curious tech-savvy users would likely prompt next: "take me to the source code" or even "contribute this feature to the server".

That would not take the user anywhere, unless the maintainers of the server thought about this ahead of time. So let's see if we can enable our server to take these users where they want to go.

The first (kind of) failed attempt at solving the problem

After learning a bit about the Model Context Protocol, my first instinct was to add some general instructions to the server metadata about how the agent should behave and also present the contribution guidelines as a server resource.

I could not find where to provide those general instructions (that's on me, it is possible), so I have tried adding that to the description of the tool "list-innersource-projects".

That was my first implementation. It kind of failed.

What I wanted to achieve was, when prompting to sort by stars, a response along the lines of: "I can't do that, but the server accepts contributions, should I contribute that feature for you?".

Instead, I got the same response as before, BUT, if I came with the explicit intent to contribute, like prompting "Can we contribute this as a feature?", the agent guided me there, and even implemented the feature and sent a pull request on my behalf.

Getting there, with the help of some robot friends

From there, I did what we are expected to do when vibe-coding these days, don't tell your coding agent what to do, tell it what you want to achieve.

A nice learning experience for me, and it came with a somewhat hacky solution. Here is what it implemented in 4 layers (its own words):

  1. Server instructions (the standing policy) - the server passes instructions to the client in the response to the server/discover query. These instructions tell the client about the open source / InnerSource features of this server, and how to react to missing features.
  2. Declared capabilities on tool responses - the response of the tool "list-innersource-projects" is a JSON data structure containing, in addition to the list of projects, a "capabilities" property. Although it looks like something a deterministic JSON parser would take and act on, it is actually telling the Large Language Model (LLM), through the client, that accepting contributions is one of the capabilities of this server.
  3. An executable action - the server offers an additional tool, "propose-contribution". Calling it does not change the state of the server in any way, but returns information to the client on how to perform a contribution.
  4. Loud, actionable failures - if the server receives a request for projects sorted by an unsupported property, it responds with an "unsupported_capability" payload carrying the requested capability, the supported contract, the contribution path, and an explicit "nextStep".
Let's see what happens now, when I try to ask the same server for a list of projects sorted by stars:
 
Screenshot of Joule Work desktop app listing InnerSource projects, and a reaction to the prompt to sort project by number of stars, stating that's not possible, but offering to contribute the missing feature.

Oh yeah! That's the Open Source and InnerSource User Experience in action. The client informs the user that the requested action is not possible, but also that the project (our server) accepts contribution, and offers help in proposing the missing feature.

Saying "Yes" here starts the journey of submitting an AI-assisted contribution to fill the gap in the server.

Conclusion and Outlook

Our little experiment showed that the state-of-the-art of agent harnesses, as MCP clients, do not drive contributions of missing features on their own. Even if you come with an intent to contribute, the harness still needs a way to discover the path to follow to make that happen. On the other hand, it also showed that it is possible to drive contributions from the server side using the current state of open standards, which is exactly what is within the sphere of control of the server's maintainers.

With this blog post, I didn't just want to demonstrate it is possible to guide users into becoming contributors, but also motivate people to think about incorporating open source and InnerSource in the user experience of what they are building. In particular, I'd like to bring this to agentic experiences.

There are still challenges ahead, like testing whether this would work if you had several MCP servers open for contributions available to the same client. Would it be able to detect in which server a feature is missing? Would it propose the contribution to the correct server and follow its corresponding contribution guidelines? Those are questions we will need to answer, in order to put this concept in use in the real world.

We also should watch carefully how the open standards for agentic engineering evolve, such as through the introduction of MCP Server Cards, which could provide open source and/or InnerSource related information to the client. Here is where the open source and InnerSource communities should also engage and influence the development of such open standards to accommodate their use cases.

Anyhow, I hope this topic sparked your interest. If this idea got your curious, you can try it yourself, the demo MCP server used to prove this concept has been open sourced: https://github.com/SAP-samples/project-aware-mcp-server 

Your feedback is very much welcome, as are your contributions! Please use the comments on this blog post or the issues on the repository to let me know your thoughts about this concept and the experiment, or in case you have anything to say about it.

entry.title: KHIVE for SAP: Process-grounded ML cells and an MCP Server for Every SAP Customer
entry.content:
Closing the gap between AI ambition and AI adoption

Picture an SAP customer where AI is simply part of the daily transaction. Every sales order carries a delivery confidence the moment it is saved. Every purchase order tells the buyer, before release, how reliable the supplier is likely to be and what to do about it. A sales representative asks Joule about an order and receives a customer-ready answer backed by the company's own history. Invoices, credit decisions and material master proposals follow the same pattern, one cell at a time, each explaining itself in the language the business already speaks. 

KHIVE for SAP will accelerate the AI adoption. A KHIVE cell is a small machine-learning model, trained on customer's S/4HANA history, that answers one business question with a probability, a label, the SAP fields that drove it and a recommended action.  With a standard way to build every model and a standard way for every agent to call it, the first cell goes live in weeks, the second reuses the first, and the catalogue grows with each project the customer already has planned. AI stops being a lab initiative and becomes part of the order desk, the purchasing team and the finance close accelerating with every use case rather than starting over.

SAP has given the ecosystem a strong answer on the agent side. Joule and the SAP Business AI platform put a capable, conversational assistant in front of every business user, and Joule Studio lets partners build agents for their customers' processes. KHIVE complements Joule by providing a framework that standardizes the development of the small, process-specific models that most SAP AI use cases actually require and a standard way to run, explain and connect them.

KHIVE is that standard framework. It is a SAP AI model framework, which gives every SAP customer the same building block, the KHIVE cell and every agent the same way to reach it via the KHIVE SAP MCP server. A cell answers one business question from the customer's own history, runs on ordinary CPU inside the customer's SAP BAIP landscape, and explains its answer in the language of the transaction. The MCP server makes every cell a tool that Joule, Joule Studio agents, or any other orchestrator can call like an SAP API.

Standardization is what turns AI from a series of projects into a capability. When every cell has the same shape, a functional consultant who delivered one for sales orders can deliver the next one for purchase orders. When every cell is reachable through the same interface, an agent built for one customer works for the next. This post shows how that plays out across three use cases, and what it means for the consultants who will carry AI into the SAP installed base.

One standard building block: the KHIVE cell

A KHIVE cell is a small, process-grounded AI/ML model framework with a fixed shape. It declares the business question it answers, the SAP fields it looks at, the historical outcome it learns from, and the recommendation a user should receive for each level of risk.  Training, scoring, explanation, metering, connectivity are provided by the framework and is identical across cells.

Because the shape is fixed, every cell exposes the same six verbs. A consultant learns them once and reuses them on every use case.

 

Verb

What it does for the business

Ingest

Reads the documents the cell learns from, through the standard S/4HANA OData APIs or a CDS view

Learn

Trains the model on the customer's own history and keeps it in the customer's landscape

Infer

Answers the question for one document or a whole worklist: a confidence score, a LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH label and a recommended action

Explain

Names the SAP fields that moved the answer, with direction and size, in the words of the transaction

Meter

Records every call and consumption

Link

Connects the cell to other cells and to agents within the company

Three properties of the standard make it adoptable at scale:

  1. It runs on CPU, inside the customer's landscape. KHIVE trains itself with remarkable efficiency.  This keeps infrastructure cost minimal and predictable, keeps the customer's data within its own landscape, and makes the business case easy to approve.
  2. It is process-grounded and taxonomy-agnostic. A cell is defined by SAP fields and an SAP outcome. Each organization brings its own process model; KHIVE adapts to it rather than imposing one.
  3. It explains itself in functional language. The explanation answers the question an experienced user would ask: what would the risk be if this field were at its normal value? The answer names a credit-check status or an availability ratio, not an anonymous feature number. That is what lets a business user trust the result, and a consultant defend it.

How it runs on SAP BTP

KHIVE runs as Cloud Foundry apps in customer's BTP subaccount, and only the cell hub talks to S/4HANA as read-only, through the Destination and Connectivity services and the Cloud Connector.

Joule reaches the cells over MCP with an XSUAA client-credentials token; business users reach the results page through the Application Router, which forwards their token so the hub checks it again. Object Store and Cloud Logging are optional: without Object Store, models retrain after each restart.

Use case 1 — Sales order delivery confidence (SD)

The question: will this sales order meet its requested delivery date?

An experienced fulfillment lead already knows the signals: the plant, the shipping condition, the credit-check status, the requested lead time, the availability situation, the order value, the number of open items, the customer's own on-time history, the material group, and whether the item is made to order. The SD consultant lists those fields, points the cell at the sales order API, and defines what "late" meant in the customer's history. The cell learns the pattern from thousands of past orders.

Where it lands for the business user

  • At order entry — the label appears on the order header when it is saved; the customer decides whether high risk is a warning or a hard stop.
  • In fulfillment monitoring — the open-order worklist is scored every night and sorted by risk, so the team starts the day with the orders that need attention.
  • In Joule — the same cell becomes the judgement behind the fulfillment agent in use case 3.

The recommendation text is written by the SD consultant in the language of the transaction release the credit block, re-run the availability check, propose a split delivery. That is functional knowledge, captured once, applied to every order by the cell.

Use case 2 — Purchase order supplier reliability (MM)

The question: will the goods receipt for this purchase order arrive on time?

The MM consultant captures the buyer's checklist: supplier tier and on-time history, Incoterms, lead time, whether the quantity is unusual for that supplier, order value, item count, material group, whether the goods are imported, and the release-strategy level. The outcome is taken from the customer's own receipts against scheduled delivery dates.

The recommendations again read like a buyer's own notes: for a new supplier, request an order acknowledgement and a firm ship date; for a supplier with a weak on-time record, add a safety lead time or dual-source the item; for a high-risk import, confirm customs documents and pre-book freight.

Where it lands for the customer

  • At PO release — the approver sees the reliability label and the suggested action beside the release strategy, before releasing.
  • In workflow — high-risk purchase orders are routed to the category buyer, or to a Joule procurement agent, for supplier follow-up.

Use case 3 — A KHIVE cell strengthening a Joule agent

The scenario. An internal sales representative asks the Joule Sales Order Fulfillment Issue Resolution agent, or an agent built in Joule Studio.

The agent can read the order, its deliveries and the customer record, and it can write an excellent reply. What it should not do is improvise a likelihood that the order will slip, and it should never put a percentage in front of a customer. So before it drafts anything, the agent makes one standard tool call to the KHIVE Joule-support cell through the MCP server, passing the order number and, where relevant, the purchase order the order depends on.

The Joule-support cell is a composite: it holds no model of its own. Using the link verb it consults the sales order cell and then returns exactly what an agent needs the delivery confidence and its drivers, the upstream supplier risk if there is one, a short list of actions ranked by owner (fulfillment, sales), and a separate set of customer-safe facts: the status phrase to use, whether the requested date may be quoted, whether a revised date must be offered.

Joule then does what Joule is for. It writes the message to the customer in the right tone, creates the follow-ups for procurement and fulfillment, and answers the representative's next question. The agent instruction is a single sentence: before any communication about an order's delivery, call the Joule-support cell and follow its customer-safe facts.

Why this pattern scales across customers

  1. The judgement is consistent. The same order returns the same confidence every time, which is what a customer commitment requires.
  2. The guardrail is in the cell, not the prompt. The cell decides what may be said to a customer; the agent decides how to say it. That separation survives prompt changes and model upgrades.

The KHIVE SAP MCP server: one interface for every agent

The Model Context Protocol is the emerging standard by which agents discover and call tools. The KHIVE SAP MCP server publishes every cell on a customer's hub as an MCP tool, with the tool description carrying the business guidance the agent needs. Joule Studio agents, the SAP Business AI platform, and any other orchestrator a customer runs can call a cell the way they call an SAP API and a cell added to the hub becomes available to all of them on the next start.

The server runs on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry behind a destination and is protected with the customer's standard app router and XSUAA. The companion project ships the deployment manifest and a Joule Studio tool definition, so a partner can stand up a customer's first hub.

This is what standardization on the model side looks like: a customer does not integrate each AI use case separately. It integrates KHIVE once, and every cell thereafter arrives through the same door.

What this means for consultants and customers

The standard framework changes who can deliver AI. Delivering a KHIVE cell is, in substance, the work a functional consultant already does for a release strategy or a pricing procedure: know the process, know the fields, say what a good decision looks like. The machine-learning part is provided by the framework and is the same for every cell.

Step

Who

What

Pick the question

Functional

One sentence, in the business's words

Choose the SAP fields

Functional

The fields an experienced user looks at, and the one or two that need a history view

Define the outcome

Functional

How the customer's history records "late", "blocked" or "breached"

Map the API

Functional + Technical

The standard OData service, plus a CDS view for history

Write the recommendations

Functional

The action per risk level, in the words of the transaction

For the customer, the result is an AI capability rather than a sequence of projects: one framework, one interface, and a growing catalogue of cells that a partner's functional team can extend.

The authors' intention

We built KHIVE with a clear purpose. Second, to give SAP consultants and forward-deployed engineers a framework they can innovate on: a standard cell that a functional consultant can specify, a standard server that any agent can call, and an open codebase that invites new cells, new industries and new ideas.

Our wider ambition is standardization. entry.title: Two New Ways to Filter Tables in SAP Analytics Cloud
entry.content:
SAP Analytics Cloud tables are getting two filtering upgrades. Filter by condition lets you filter the table by a rule. Beyond that, filtering by condition and member are getting new entry points. Both filter options are now available directly from the column header context menu, in edit and view mode.

 

Filter by Condition

 

Filter by condition is new for tables. It lets you filter which dimension members are shown based on a condition, such as showing only members that start with or contain a certain string. This is different from filtering by members, which narrows to specific selected values. Charts and geomaps have had conditional filtering for a while. Tables now reach parity with the other widget types.

 

Conditional filters can be added from the builder panel (both the filters section and the dimension token), or directly from the dimension header context menu using Filter Options > Filter By Condition as we will show in more detail in the next section.
 
                         Add filter from dimension tokenAdd filter in the filter section

 

A new entry point for both filter types

 

Our second filtering update is a new entry point for the available filters: Just like Filter by Condition, the existing Filter by Member is now accessible from the column header context menu. Right-clicking a dimension header shows filter options directly, without opening the builder panel.

Add a filter from the dimension header

Filters applied this way show up in the table details panel and in the Applied to Table area, exactly as if you had added them through the builder. The behaviour is consistent whether you come in from the header or the panel. Both filter types are available in edit and view mode, so story viewers can filter directly from the header without needing edit access.

 

What changes for each audience

 

For end users, filtering just got more powerful and easier to find. Until now, they were only able to filter via the members directly in the cell and multi-selection was at times cumbersome. Filtering from the header allows more flexibility and speeds up the process. And the new option of conditional filters makes this even more powerful.

 

For consultants building stories, it simplifies design. You don't need to pre-configure every possible filter into the story, because viewers can set their own from the header, member-based or condition-based. For IT teams, it's a capability that reduces the round-trip to the story designer when a business user needs a different slice of the data.

 

Both features are available on the new table build experience. We are planning on following up in the next quarters with two more functionalities that are not yet supported like filter from header for measures and the time range filter in view mode.

 

Are there filtering scenarios in your SAC tables that these changes don't cover yet? Drop a comment below — I'd love to hear what you're working with today and what you still need.

entry.title: Re: populate Payment Reference Field from Vendor Invoice...
entry.content:
Hello,

Thank you very much for your question.

Here is the response our internal chatbot has provided. Please check which of the approaches work best for you.

Kind regards,

Henrike

#AI-Generated Content

Payment Reference Field Population: Vendor Invoice → Payment Document (ZP)

This is a known behavioral limitation in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. By design, the automatic payment program does not transfer the Payment Reference (BSEG-KIDNO) or other reference fields from the supplier invoice to the payment document (ZP). This applies even in 1:1 payment scenarios, because a single payment can clear multiple invoices with differing reference values, making the transfer non-deterministic. [1]

Key Field Mapping
Source Target Standard Behavior
Vendor Invoice – Payment Reference (BSEG-KIDNO)Payment Document ZP – Payment Reference❌ Not transferred automatically by design [1]
Vendor Invoice – Reference Field (BKPF-XBLNR)Payment Document ZP – Reference Field❌ Not transferred automatically by design [1]
Root Cause & Design Behavior

SAP KBA 3735929 explicitly confirms: "By design, the automatic payment program does not transfer invoice Reference or Assignment values to the payment document. Because a payment can clear multiple invoices with differing values, copying a single Reference is non-deterministic." [1]

Additionally, for SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud specifically:

  • The Payment Reference field (BSEG-KIDNO) is not exposed for substitution through available frameworks such as BAdI FIN_ACDOC_ITEM_SUBSTITUTION or the Manage Substitution and Validation Rules app. [2]
  • In the private cloud environment, BSEG-KIDNO is explicitly excluded from substitution rules via the BEXCLUDE indicator in table GB01. [3]

⚠️ Important for Sweden (Public Cloud): The substitution-based approach (copying RGGBS000 to ZRGGBS000 and using GGB1) that works in on-premise or private cloud is not available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition due to extensibility restrictions. [2]

Available Options in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition

Option 1: Vote on the Feature Request (Recommended First Step) SAP has raised Feature Request ID 370767 on the SAP Customer Influence portal specifically for transferring reference fields from invoice to payment document. [1]

  • Navigate to: https://influence.sap.com/sap/ino/#/idea/370767
  • Vote for this request to accelerate SAP's review and delivery.

Option 2: Sweden-Specific OCR/Payment Reference Validation For Sweden, the system applies country-specific validation on the Payment Reference field (BSEG-KIDNO) at the time of supplier invoice entry: [4] [5]

  • Message F0 468: "Payment reference &2 is incorrect for Sweden" — this is a hard error by default.
  • If free use of the payment reference is required, configure it as a warning via:
    • SSCUI ID: 106990 – Change Message Control – Payments
    • Application Area: F0, Message Number: 468, set to W (Warning). [4]

Option 3: Custom Reference Fields in Payment Medium Format For payment file generation purposes, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition allows including custom reference fields in the payment medium format: [6]

  • Use the Map Format Data for Payments configuration activity.
  • Custom fields can be mapped to the payment format structure.
  • This addresses the payment file/medium output but does not populate the ZP document's internal reference field.

Option 4: Sweden Payment Method Configuration (SEPA Credit Transfer) Ensure the Sweden payment method is correctly configured with the Note to Payee by Origin setting assigned to SAP_CGI for Sweden CGI format remittance information. [7] This controls remittance data in the payment file (pain.001), not the ZP document reference field itself.

Configuration Steps (for Message Control Workaround – Sweden)
  1. Open Configure Your Solution → search for "Change Message Control – Payments" (SSCUI ID: 106990).
  2. Select Application Area: F0 (FI batch program messages).
  3. Create or adjust an entry for Message Number 468.
  4. Set the message type to W (Warning) to allow free entry of payment reference on supplier invoices for Sweden. [4]
Sweden-Specific Considerations
  • In Sweden, the Payment Reference (BSEG-KIDNO) is checked with country-specific logic (check digit validation). The system forwards the payment reference in payment transactions only if the business partner/payee, bank of the payee, house bank of the company code, and correspondence banks involved all have their registered offices in Sweden. [5]
  • For outbound billing documents (customer invoices), Sweden uses the OCR Number as the reference — one extra random digit is added to the invoice number, and this reference is passed to the journal entry header. This is a separate flow from the Accounts Payable/vendor invoice scenario. [8]
  • The Document Information Extraction (OCR) feature (INV-386) automatically extracts the Payment Reference field from inbound supplier invoices for Nordic countries including Sweden — this populates the draft invoice field, but does not resolve the transfer to the ZP payment document. [9]
Summary
Approach Feasibility in S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition Addresses ZP Reference Field?
Automatic transfer by payment program❌ Not supported by design [1]No
Substitution (GGB1/RGGBS000)❌ Not available in Public Cloud [2]No
Feature Request 370767 (Vote)✅ Recommended path [1]Future delivery
Message Control SSCUI 106990✅ AvailableAllows free entry on invoice only
Custom Reference Fields in Payment Medium✅ Available [6]Payment file only, not ZP document

The most actionable path for your Sweden company code is to vote on Feature Request 370767 and, in the interim, ensure the payment reference is correctly entered on the supplier invoice (with message control set to Warning if needed) so it is available for manual reconciliation or payment medium output.

entry.title: SAP Document and Reporting Compliance: e-Invoice in Contract Accounting (FI-CA) using Extensibility
entry.content:
You want to enable your system to create electronic documents for invoices posted via Contract Accounting (FI-CA) using SAP Document and Reporting Compliance. In this blog, we'll show you an example of how this can be achieved using extensibility, with the Netherlands (NL) as a reference country.

Before you begin, ensure that the Financial Accounting Document, Sales and Distribution Billing Document e-Invoicing option is already available in your system for the specific country, including the eDocument customization and eDocument process. An implementation overview note (ex: for NL 2424637 ) will be available for each country e-Invoicing process if the country is localized by SAP for Financial Accounting Document, Sales and Distribution Billing Document. If you need to set up e-Invoicing from scratch for your country without an existing FI/SD localization, refer to Extensibility for Electronic Document Processing in Private Cloud.

Implement the following SAP Notes before proceeding:

3337374, 3342537, 3331737, 3332372, 3381485, 3387690, 3406988, 3413057, 3406213 — these notes enable e-invoice for Contract Accounting and trigger eDocument creation from all relevant transaction codes.

Important: Download and activate the BC Sets attached to notes 3331737 and 3381485.

Steps to Create Electronic Documents

1. Configure the eDocument Type Table

Customize the eDocument: Accounting Document Type for FI-CA view (V_TFK003EDOC2) for your country to determine the eDocument type based on the type of FI-CA document.

Example configuration for Country/Region NL:

Replace NL_INV and NL_CRE with the eDocument types defined for your country (e.g. XX_INV, XX_CRE).

2. Create the eDocument Class

Create a new class ZCL_EDOCUMENT_XX_CA (replace XX with your country code) and set the superclass to CL_EDOCUMENT_EU_CA if you use the PEPPOL network, or CL_EDOCUMENT_XX for others. 

Example for NL — class CL_EDOCUMENT_NL_CA with superclass CL_EDOCUMENT_EU_CA.

Add a CONSTRUCTOR method with the following parameters:

                            iv_generic_badi_filter_adaptor = COND edoc_generic_badi_filter(

                                                               THEN iv_generic_badi_filter_adaptor
                                                               ELSE cl_edoc_source_fica_document=>gc_src_fica_document ) ).

Redefine the following methods:

DETERMINE_PROCESS — assigns the correct process and process version based on the eDocument type and interface type. Replace NL with your country of choice.

        ).

METHOD process_request_send.

    DATA: lv_variant                    TYPE edoc_proc_step_variant,
          lv_is_procstepvar_overwritten TYPE abap_bool.

    TRY.
        get_proc_step_variant(

                    ev_is_procstepvar_overwritten = lv_is_procstepvar_overwritten ).

        super->process_request_send(
          EXPORTING
            iv_interface_guid = iv_interface_guid

With these settings you should be able to create an eDocument and view it in transaction EDOC_COCKPIT.

3. Create the AIF Mapping Class

Create a mapping class ZCL_EDOC_MAP_UBL_CA_XX for your country.

  • For PEPPOL countries: set the superclass to CL_EDOC_MAP_UBL_CA.
  • For non-PEPPOL countries: set the superclass to CL_EDOC_MAP_XX
